# RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner

###### Abstract

The reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs) have improved
with chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, allowing models to solve complex
tasks stepwise. However, training CoT capabilities requires detailed
reasoning data, which is often scarce. The self-taught reasoner (STaR)
framework addresses this by using reinforcement learning to
automatically generate reasoning steps, reducing reliance on
human-labeled data. Although STaR and its variants have demonstrated
empirical success, a theoretical foundation explaining these
improvements is lacking. This work provides a theoretical framework for
understanding the effectiveness of reinforcement learning on CoT
reasoning and STaR. Our contributions are: (1) criteria for the quality
of pre-trained models necessary to initiate effective reasoning
improvement; (2) an analysis of policy improvement, showing why LLM
reasoning improves iteratively with STaR; (3) conditions for convergence
to an optimal reasoning policy; and (4) an examination of STaR’s
robustness, explaining how it can improve reasoning even when
incorporating occasional incorrect steps. We also run RL-STaR on GPT-2,
Qwen2.5-0.5B and Phi-3-mini, and the measured return curves follow the
ones the analysis predicts. This framework bridges empirical findings
with theoretical insights, advancing reinforcement learning approaches
for reasoning in LLMs.

## 1 Introduction

With the advancement of large language models (LLMs), their reasoning
capabilities have become crucial to their success. This progress is
mainly attributed to chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting ([Wei et al.,
2022](#bib.bib1)), which allows LLMs to go beyond pattern matching and
handle more complex reasoning problems by providing step-by-step
guidance. GPT4-o1 ([OpenAI, 2024](#bib.bib17)) exemplifies this success,
achieving high scores on various mathematical and programming
benchmarks. However, to train models with CoT capabilities, training
data must include detailed reasoning steps ([Malach, 2024](#bib.bib2);
[Prystawski et al., 2024](#bib.bib3); [Xiao and Liu, 2024](#bib.bib4)),
which are often absent. To address this challenge, the self-taught
reasoner (STaR) approach ([Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib11)) was
proposed, leveraging reinforcement learning to automatically discover
reasoning steps. Numerous improvements to STaR have since been
introduced ([Hosseini et al., 2024](#bib.bib13); [Zelikman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib12); [Lin et al., 2025](#bib.bib26); [Andukuri et al.,
2024](#bib.bib27); [Xiang et al., 2025](#bib.bib14)), demonstrating
empirically that LLMs can effectively learn reasoning steps via
reinforcement learning without human intervention. Although some
theoretical research exists on CoT techniques (e.g., ([Prystawski et
al., 2024](#bib.bib3); [Malach, 2024](#bib.bib2); [Feng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib5); [Xiao and Liu, 2024](#bib.bib4); [Hu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib29))), these studies are primarily focused on supervised
and auto-regressive learning settings that require detailed reasoning
steps included in training data. They do not show how reinforcement
learning techniques can enhance reasoning steps. Furthermore, while
there are existing reinforcement learning frameworks for theoretical
analysis (e.g., ([Jin et al., 2018](#bib.bib7); [Ayoub et al.,
2020](#bib.bib15); [Jin et al., 2021](#bib.bib6); [Jin et al.,
2020](#bib.bib8); [Bhandari and Russo, 2021](#bib.bib16); [Chen et al.,
2022](#bib.bib10); [Yeh et al., 2023](#bib.bib18); [Lai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib19))), none are designed to analyze the self-improvement
of LLMs through reinforcement learning. As a result, no theoretical
framework explains how LLMs can enhance their reasoning capabilities via
reinforcement learning. A detailed literature review is given in
Sec. [2](#S2 "2 Related Works ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").

### 1.1 Our Contributions

In this work, we develop a theoretical framework to analyze how the
Self-Taught Reasoner (STaR) enhances Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning
under a simplified setup such as Markov properties (see
Sec. [6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Markov Assumption of State Transitions ‣ 6 Limitations and Possible Extensions ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")).
In this context, we address the following questions:

1.  1.  Conditions of Pre-trained Models for STaR: _How competent does the
        pre-trained LLM need to be to bootstrap the discovery of reasoning
        steps in the first iteration?_ We show that a pre-trained LLM can
        initiate effective reasoning improvement if one of the following
        holds when inferencing on the problems in STaR’s training set.
    - •
      The pre-trained LLM performs better than a randomly initialized
      model at each reasoning step (i.e., its probability of producing
      the correct step exceeds that of random guessing).
    - •
      The pre-trained LLM is on par with a randomly initialized model at
      exactly one reasoning step but exceeds it at all other steps.

2.  2.  Policy Improvement: _Can LLMs improve their reasoning capabilities
        iteratively through STaR?_ We demonstrate that if the pre-trained
        model satisfies the conditions we mentioned previously, within each
        iteration of the STaR algorithm, LLMs can consistently improve the
        correctness of their reasoning trajectories.
3.  3.  Convergence to the Optimal Policy: _If an optimal reasoning model
        exists, can STaR eventually find this optimal reasoner?_ Given
        sufficient iterations, we prove that if the pre-trained model
        satisfies the previously mentioned conditions, LLMs can converge to
        the optimal reasoner, achieving the highest probability of
        generating correct reasoning trajectories that lead to correct
        answers.
4.  4.  Existence of Incorrect Reasoning Steps in STaR: _Is it possible for
        a sub-optimal model to generate incorrect reasoning steps that are
        included in the next iteration of training, while still arriving at
        the correct final answer?_ We show that even when incorrect
        reasoning steps are included in the training data for a given
        iteration, the probability of these incorrect reasoning steps being
        included in the training data will diminish as the number of STaR
        iterations increases.

Although our theoretical setup simplifies real-world LLM settings, we
also discuss how our theoretical results could be applied to more
realistic scenarios. In
Sec. [4.5](#S4.SS5 "4.5 Comparison with the Convergence Analysis of Policy-Gradient Methods ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
we explain why the convergence guarantees of policy-gradient methods do
not already answer these questions.

## 2 Related Works

### 2.1 Approaches to Improve Chain-of-Thought

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves reasoning by encouraging
models to generate intermediate steps ([Wei et al., 2022](#bib.bib1)).
However, scaling model size alone does not strengthen causal
understanding [Bao et al. (2025)](#bib.bib33), motivating research on
selecting effective CoT prompts and correcting flawed reasoning traces
(e.g., [Jiang et al. (2024)](#bib.bib34)). Recent work has explored
multiple strategies for enhancing CoT. Retrieval-Q-CoT ([Zhang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib32)) selects prompts by grouping questions via cosine
similarity, while Process Supervision ([Lightman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28)) trains reward models that stabilize step-by-step
reasoning. Other studies focus on discovering optimal instructions
([Zhou et al., 2023](#bib.bib36)) or improving Zero-Shot CoT through
automated prompting strategies ([Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib35)).
Importantly, [Huang et al. (2024)](#bib.bib37) shows that external
feedback is critical for self-correction, highlighting the need for
explicit feedback-driven mechanisms. Overall, these approaches
illustrate a growing effort to refine CoT prompting, enhance reasoning
robustness, and reduce reliance on model scale alone.

### 2.2 Self-Taught Reasoner (STaR) for Boosting Chain-of-Thought

The Self-Taught Reasoner (STaR) framework ([Zelikman et al.,
2022](#bib.bib11)) improves LLM reasoning by using reinforcement
learning to iteratively refine self-generated chain-of-thought (CoT)
traces. STaR first produces reasoning steps via in-context learning,
retains only those leading to correct answers, and continually expands
its training set with successful CoTs. Numerous extensions enhance this
paradigm: Quiet-STaR ([Zelikman et al., 2024](#bib.bib12)) adds
token-level rationales; V-STaR ([Hosseini et al., 2024](#bib.bib13))
trains a verifier using DPO to assess both correct and incorrect
solutions; Lean-STaR ([Lin et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)) introduces
informal pre-proof reasoning; STaR-GATE ([Andukuri et al.,
2024](#bib.bib27)) rewards insightful question generation; and Meta-STaR
([Xiang et al., 2025](#bib.bib14)) incorporates meta-cognitive CoT.
Other variants include B-STaR ([Zeng et al., 2025](#bib.bib45)), which
balances exploration and exploitation, and rStar-Math ([Guan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib46)), showing strong reasoning gains even for small
models. Despite these advances, the theoretical basis for why STaR
enables autonomous reasoning improvement remains largely unexplored.

### 2.3 Theories of Reinforcement Learning

Reinforcement learning theory aims to explain how algorithms iteratively
improve a policy toward optimality. Foundational results on Tabular
Q-learning, such as ([Jin et al., 2018](#bib.bib7)), establish
polynomial-time convergence, with extensions to settings involving
linear reward and transition structures ([Jin et al., 2020](#bib.bib8);
[Yang and Wang, 2019](#bib.bib21); [He et al., 2021](#bib.bib20)) and
kernel-based function approximation ([Yang et al., 2020](#bib.bib9);
[Yeh et al., 2023](#bib.bib18)). Additional analyses characterize
convergence for policy gradient methods ([Phansalkar and Thathachar,
1995](#bib.bib47); [Bhandari and Russo, 2021](#bib.bib16); [Bhandari and
Russo, 2024](#bib.bib22)), human-in-the-loop RL ([Chen et al.,
2022](#bib.bib10); [Kong and Yang, 2022](#bib.bib23)), model-based RL
([Osband and Van Roy, 2014](#bib.bib24); [Ayoub et al.,
2020](#bib.bib15)), and offline RL ([Hu et al., 2023](#bib.bib25); [Jin
et al., 2021](#bib.bib6); [Lai et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)). Collectively,
these works provide deep insight into classical RL algorithms and their
sample-efficiency guarantees. However, they do not directly address the
distinct challenges involved in improving large language model
reasoning—where policies correspond to multi-step generative processes
rather than state-action mappings. This gap motivates the need for new
theoretical frameworks tailored to RL-driven enhancement of
chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs.

### 2.4 Theories of Chain-of-Thought

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting ([Wei et al., 2022](#bib.bib1)) enables
LLMs to solve complex tasks by decomposing solutions into stepwise
reasoning. Several theoretical works attempt to explain its
effectiveness. [Prystawski et al. (2024)](#bib.bib3) models CoT as
Bayesian networks linking questions, answers, and intermediate steps,
while [Xiao and Liu (2024)](#bib.bib4) introduces length generalization,
showing that models can extend simple patterns to harder cases. In a PAC
auto-regressive framework, [Malach (2024)](#bib.bib2) proves that CoT
allows learning linear threshold circuits. CoT also increases
computational reach: [Feng et al. (2024)](#bib.bib5) demonstrates
transformer ability to emulate dynamic programming; [Li et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib30) and [Kim and Suzuki (2025)](#bib.bib31) show
enhanced expressiveness via sequential intermediate states. Additional
analyses address sample complexity ([Hu et al., 2024](#bib.bib29); [Li
et al., 2025](#bib.bib42)), OOD generalization ([Yao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib43)), and the role of positional embeddings ([Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41)). While these studies form the theoretical basis of
CoT, they do not explain why reinforcement learning further improves
CoT, nor how to reduce reliance on extensive reasoning-step supervision.

## 3 Theoretical Framework

### 3.1 Problem Formulation

In our problem formulation, we consider a chain of thought (CoT)
reasoning process composed of $`N`$ steps where $`N>1`$. Let $`s_{0}`$
denote the initial input string, and $`s_{n}`$ represent the resulting
string after the $`n`$-th CoT step, where $`1\leq n\leq N`$. We assume
that the chain-of-thought steps satisfy the Markov property: each string
$`s_{n}`$ contains sufficient information to derive the next string
$`s_{n+1}`$, without relying on information from any of the preceding
strings $`s_{i}`$ where $`0\leq i<n`$. For instance, in the addition
problem $`1+2+3+4`$, the chain-of-thought steps can be expressed as:

|     |     |                                                                                                                                       |     |
| --- | --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle s_{0}=\texttt{1+2+3+4}\Rightarrow s_{1}=\texttt{3+3+4}~\Rightarrow s_{2}=\texttt{6+4}\Rightarrow s_{3}=\texttt{10}.`$ |     |

In this example, obtaining $`s_{2}=\texttt{6+4}`$ requires only the
information in $`s_{1}=\texttt{3+3+4}`$ and does not depend on
$`s_{0}=\texttt{1+2+3+4}`$. Under this Markov assumption, the
chain-of-thought (CoT) process can naturally be cast as a Reinforcement
Learning (RL) problem, which can be described by a Markov decision
process (MDP). Formally, let
$`\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},N,r,\mathcal{P})`$ represent the
MDP, where:

- •
  $`\mathcal{S}`$ is the space of all possible initial inputs, CoT
  steps, and final answers, denoted $`\{s_{i}\mid 0\leq i\leq N\}`$. In
  this formulation, $`s_{0}`$ is the CoT input, $`s_{1},\ldots,s_{N-1}`$
  are the subsequent reasoning steps, and $`s_{N}`$ is the final answer.
- •
  $`\mathcal{A}`$ is the action space. Because each action corresponds
  uniquely to selecting the next state, we identify $`\mathcal{A}`$ with
  $`\mathcal{S}`$. That is, choosing $`a`$ is equivalent to setting
  $`s_{n+1}`$ as the unique next step associated with $`a`$.
- •
  $`\mathcal{P}`$ is the transition function. Given that an action $`a`$
  uniquely determines the next state $`s_{n+1}`$, this transition is
  deterministic:

  |     |     |     |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  |     |

  ````math
  \mathcal{P}\bigl(S_{n+1}=s_{n+1}\big|A=s_{n+1},S_{n}=s_{n}\bigr)=1.
  ``` |  |
  ````

- •
  $`r(s_{0},s_{N})`$ is the reward function, yielding a nonzero reward
  solely at the final step if $`s_{N}`$ matches the correct answer.
  Concretely, consider a dataset $`\mathcal{D}`$ composed of
  question-answer pairs. For each instance
  $`(s_{0},s_{N}^{\star})\in\mathcal{D}`$, where $`s_{0}`$ represents
  the question and $`s_{N}^{\star}`$ the correct final answer, define

  |     |     |     |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  |     |

  ````math
  r(s_{0},s_{N})=\begin{cases}1,~\text{if $s_{N}=s_{N}^{\star}$ and $(s_{0},s_{N}^{\star})\in\mathcal{D}$},\\
  0,~\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
  ``` |  |

  Thus, the agent earns a reward of 1 exclusively when it terminates on
  $`s_{N}^{\star}`$, and 0 otherwise. Note that we fixed the number of
  CoT steps to be $`N`$; intermediate states $`s_{n}`$ (for
  $`1\leq n<N`$) do not produce any positive reward.
  ````

Given the RL formulation above, a policy $`\pi(A\mid S_{n}=s_{n})`$
specifies how the next action $`A=s_{n+1}`$ is selected based on the
current state $`S_{n}=s_{n}`$. Although the transition
$`\mathcal{P}\bigl(S_{n+1}\mid A=s_{n+1},S_{n}=s_{n}\bigr)`$ is
deterministic (that is, once $`A=s_{n+1}`$ is chosen,
$`S_{n+1}=s_{n+1}`$ is uniquely determined), the policy
$`\pi(A\mid S_{n}=s_{n})`$ itself can be stochastic if there is
uncertainty about which next step to choose given $`S_{n}=s_{n}`$. To
streamline notations, we define a stochastic transition
$`P(S_{n+1}\mid S_{n})`$ by combining the stochastic policy
$`\pi(A\mid S_{n})`$ with the deterministic transition
$`\mathcal{P}(S_{n+1}\mid A,S_{n})`$:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
P\bigl(S_{n+1}\mid S_{n}\bigr)\;=\;\mathcal{P}\bigl(S_{n+1}\mid\pi(A\mid S_{n}),S_{n}\bigr).
``` |  |

In this setup, the LLM serves as the transition function
$`P(S_{n+1}\mid S_{n})`$, producing the subsequent CoT step $`s_{n+1}`$
based on the current CoT step $`s_{n}`$. After the final step $`s_{N}`$
is reached, the reward function $`r(s_{0},s_{N})`$ measures correctness
by comparing $`s_{N}`$ to the ground truth answer $`s_{N}^{\star}`$.

 Input: A dataset
$`\mathcal{D}=\{(s_{0}^{(k)},s_{N}^{\star(k)})|k\in[K]\}`$, a
pre-trained LLM as transition $`P_{0}`$.

 Output: A trained LLM as transition $`P_{T}`$.

 for $`t=1`$ to $`T`$ do

  $`\#`$ Repeat the following procedure for $`L`$ times where
$`L\gg K`$.

  for $`\ell=1`$ to $`L`$ do

   $`\left(s_{0}^{(\ell)}s_{N}^{\star(\ell)}\right)\sim\mathcal{D}`$.
$`\#`$ Uniformly sample a pair
$`\left(s_{0}^{(\ell)},s_{N}^{\star(\ell)}\right)`$ from
$`\mathcal{D}`$.

   $`\tau^{(\ell)}\leftarrow(s_{0}^{(\ell)},)`$ $`\#`$ Set
$`s_{0}^{(\ell)}`$ as the initial state of the trajectory
$`\tau^{(\ell)}`$.

   for $`n=1`$ to $`N`$ do

    $`s_{n}^{(\ell)}\sim P_{t-1}(S_{n}|S_{n-1}=s_{n-1}^{(\ell)})`$
$`\#`$ Randomly sample $`s_{n}^{(\ell)}`$ with probability
$`P_{t-1}(S_{n}=s_{n}^{(\ell)}|S_{n-1}=s_{n-1}^{(\ell)})`$.

    $`\tau^{(\ell)}\leftarrow(\tau^{(\ell)}_{1:n-1},s_{n}^{(\ell)})`$
$`\#`$ Append $`s_{n}^{(\ell)}`$ to $`\tau^{(\ell)}`$.

   end for

  end for

  $`\mathcal{D}_{t}\leftarrow\left\{\tau^{(\ell)}\mid\ell\in[L]\text{ and }s_{N}^{(\ell)}=s_{N}^{\star(\ell)}\right\}`$
$`\#`$ Add the trajectories whose final state $`s_{N}^{(\ell)}`$ matches
$`s_{N}^{\star(\ell)}`$ to $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$.

  $`P_{t}\leftarrow\operatorname{Train}\left(P_{t-1},\mathcal{D}_{t}\right)`$
$`\#`$ Use $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$ to update the transition.

 end for

Algorithm 1 RL-STaR

To guide LLMs toward selecting a final state $`s_{N}`$ that maximizes
the reward upon completing CoT, we use a modified version of
STaR ([Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib11)), termed RL-STaR, as outlined
in Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 3 Theoretical Framework ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
This algorithm takes a training dataset $`\mathcal{D}`$ and a
pre-trained LLM as transition $`P_{0}`$ as input, and outputs a trained
LLM as transition $`P_{T}`$, where $`\mathcal{D}`$ consists of $`K`$
instances. In each iteration $`t`$, we repeat the following procedure
$`L`$ times: we uniformly sample a pair
$`\bigl(s_{0}^{(\ell)},s_{N}^{\star(\ell)}\bigr)`$ from $`\mathcal{D}`$
and generate a trajectory $`\tau^{(\ell)}`$ by sequentially sampling
states from the current transition $`P_{t-1}`$. Specifically, starting
from $`s_{0}^{(\ell)}`$, we iteratively draw
$`s_{n}^{(\ell)}\sim P_{t-1}\bigl(S_{n}\!\mid\!S_{n-1}=s_{n-1}^{(\ell)}\bigr)`$
for $`n=1,\dots,N`$. If the final state $`s_{N}^{(\ell)}`$ matches the
ground truth $`s_{N}^{\star(\ell)}`$, we add the entire trajectory
$`\tau^{(\ell)}`$ to $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$. After completing these $`L`$
samplings, we update $`P_{t-1}`$ to $`P_{t}`$ by retraining on
$`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$. In particular,
$`\operatorname{Train}(P_{t-1},\mathcal{D}_{t})`$ adjusts the transition
probabilities $`P_{t-1}(S_{n}=s_{n}\!\mid\!S_{n-1}=s_{n-1})`$ to better
align with the transitions observed in the successful trajectories
within $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$. After $`T`$ iterations, this procedure
outputs the final transition model $`P_{T}`$. In
Sec. [4](#S4 "4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
we show that RL-STaR aims to maximize the total expected return
$`J(P_{t})`$, defined by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle J(P_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{(s_{0},s_{N}^{\star})\sim\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{E}_{(s_{1},\cdots,s_{N})\sim P_{t}(\tau|S_{0}=s_{0})}r(s_{0},s_{N}),`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\text{where}~P_{t}(\tau|S_{0}=s_{0})=P_{t}(S_{1}=s_{1}|S_{0}=s_{0})\times(\Pi_{n=2}^{N}P_{t}(S_{n}=s_{n}|S_{n-1}=s_{n-1})).`$ |  |

### 3.2 Settings of Our Theoretical Analysis

##### Markov Assumption of Language Models’ Input

For simplicity in analyzing the RL-STaR algorithm, we impose the Markov
assumption by allowing the LLM to accept only the current step
$`s_{n-1}`$ as input, rather than the complete history
$`\bigl(s_{0},s_{1},\dots,s_{n-2}\bigr)`$. This contrasts with standard
CoT methods, which include every previous token in the context.
Nevertheless, the Markov property remains essential for CoT
generalization. Several studies (e.g., ([Yao et al., 2025](#bib.bib43);
[Teng et al., 2025](#bib.bib44); [Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib41); [Li et
al., 2025](#bib.bib42); [Xiao and Liu, 2024](#bib.bib4); [Prystawski et
al., 2024](#bib.bib3))) show that CoT succeeds by breaking complex tasks
into simpler, reusable subtasks whose outcomes depend only on a limited
recent context, thus preserving Markovian structure. The details are
discussed in
Sec. [6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Markov Assumption of State Transitions ‣ 6 Limitations and Possible Extensions ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").

##### Simplification of STaR Algorithm

For simplicity in our theoretical analysis, we exclude the
*rationalization* from STaR—that is, we do not correct an LLM’s
incorrect outputs using hints derived from the final answer. As noted in
([Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib11)), omitting rationalization may
reduce STaR’s convergence rate. However, based on their result,
rationalization is not a necessary condition for policy improvement.
Hence, we accept this trade-off here since our focus lies on preliminary
theoretical examination rather than achieving state-of-the-art
performance on reasoning benchmarks.

##### Assumption of the Ground-Truth Reasoner $`\bar{\pi}`$

We assume that a ground-truth transition $`\bar{P}(S_{n+1}|S_{n})`$
exists, which produces the correct sequence $`s_{1},\ldots,s_{N-1}`$
leading to $`s_{N}=s_{N}^{\star}`$ given $`s_{0}`$ for every instance
$`(s_{0},s_{N}^{\star})`$ in $`\mathcal{D}`$. This property enables us
to apply the analysis of RL-STaR which approximates
$`\bar{P}(S_{n+1}|S_{n})`$ with an estimated transition
$`P_{T}(s_{n+1}|S_{n})`$. It is clear that if an estimated transition
$`P_{T}`$ can perfectly match the ground-truth reasoning step
transitions $`\bar{P}`$, it would be the optimal estimated transition
$`P^{\star}`$ which maximizes $`J(P^{\star})`$, namely,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle P^{\star}(S_{n+1}=s_{n+1}|S_{n}=s_{n})=\bar{P}(S_{n+1}=s_{n+1}|S_{n}=s_{n}),`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\text{\quad for all $(s_{n+1},s_{n})\in\operatorname{support}{(S_{n+1})}\times\operatorname{support}{(S_{n})}$,\, where }n\in\{0,1,\dots,N-1\}.`$ |  |

## 4 Theoretical Results

In this section, we present our theoretical analysis addressing the
questions outlined in
Sec. [1.1](#S1.SS1 "1.1 Our Contributions ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
We outline conditions under which the RL-STaR algorithm can effectively
train an LLM to approximate the optimal estimated transition
$`P^{\star}`$.

### 4.1 Notations

For clarity, the notations used in the main text are presented below.
The additional notation that appears only in the proofs is collected
in [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Additional Notation ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").

- •
  $`T`$, $`N`$, $`M`$: the number of RL-STaR iterations, the number of
  CoT steps, and the number of states at each CoT step.
- •
  $`s_{n,m}`$: the $`m`$-th state at the $`n`$-th CoT step, and
  $`s_{n,m^{\prime}\neq m}`$: any state at the $`n`$-th CoT step other
  than $`s_{n,m}`$.
- •
  $`[n]`$: the set $`\{1,2,\dots,n\}`$, and
  $`\operatorname{support}(S)`$: the support of a random variable $`S`$.
- •
  $`\tau=(s_{0},s_{1},\dots,s_{N})`$: a trajectory, written as a tuple
  whose entries appear in the order listed.
- •
  $`[P]_{i,j}`$: the element with index $`(i,j)`$ in the matrix $`P`$;
  $`I_{M}`$: the $`M\times M`$ identity matrix; and $`e_{1}`$: the first
  standard basis vector.
- •
  $`\|P\|_{\infty}`$: the induced $`\infty`$-norm of the matrix $`P`$,
  that is, $`\|P\|_{\infty}=\max_{i}\sum_{j}\left|[P]_{i,j}\right|`$.
- •
  $`\lceil x\rceil_{+}`$:
  $`\operatorname{min}(\{n\mid n\in\mathbb{N}~\text{and}~n\geq x\})`$,
  and $`\lfloor x\rfloor_{+}`$:
  $`\operatorname{max}(\{n\mid n\in\mathbb{N}~\text{and}~n\leq x\})`$,
  where $`\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\dots\}`$.
- •
  $`\mathbb{I}\{a=b\}`$ : $`\mathbb{I}\{a=b\}=1`$ if $`a=b`$; otherwise
  $`\mathbb{I}\{a=b\}=0`$.

### 4.2 The Family $`P_{n}[\delta]`$ and Standing Assumptions

Throughout
Sec. [4](#S4 "4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
a CoT step $`n`$ has $`M`$ states. We write $`\bar{P}_{n}`$ for the
ground-truth transition at that step, which puts all of its mass on the
correct next state, and $`P_{u,n}`$ for the uniform transition, which
puts mass $`\frac{1}{M}`$ on every state.

###### Definition 4.1 ($`\delta`$-accurate transition).

For $`\delta\in[0,1)`$, let

|     |                                                             |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       P_{n}[\delta]\;:=\;\delta\,\bar{P}_{n}+(1-\delta)\,P_{u,n},
       ```                                                          |     |

so that $`P_{n}[\delta]`$ assigns probability
$`\frac{1+(M-1)\delta}{M}`$ to the correct next step and
$`\frac{1-\delta}{M}`$ to each of the $`M-1`$ incorrect ones. Hence
$`P_{n}[0]=P_{u,n}`$ is the uniform model, and $`P_{n}[\delta]`$
approaches $`\bar{P}_{n}`$ as $`\delta\rightarrow 1`$, so $`\delta`$
measures how far the model has moved from random guessing toward the
ground-truth reasoner.

The results in this section rest on two assumptions about RL-STaR.

###### Assumption 4.2 (Training set).

$`\mathcal{D}=\{(s_{0,m},s_{N,m})\mid m\in[M]\}`$, that is, the training
set holds one question–answer pair per ground-truth trajectory.

###### Assumption 4.3 (Exact fitting).

$`\operatorname{Train}(P_{t-1},\mathcal{D}_{t})`$ returns the transition
that matches the conditional distribution of $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$
exactly. That is, for every step $`n`$, $`P_{t,n}(S_{n}\mid S_{n-1})`$
equals the conditional probability of observing $`(s_{n-1,m},s_{n,m})`$
and $`(s_{n-1,m},s_{n,m^{\prime}\neq m})`$ among the trajectories
$`\tau\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}`$.

### 4.3 A Toy Example

We first illustrate our theoretical results with a toy example. In this
scenario, we consider a CoT process with two reasoning steps (i.e.,
$`N=2`$), and each step has two possible states (i.e., $`M=2`$). Here,
$`S_{0}`$ is a random variable representing the initial state, $`S_{1}`$
the intermediate state, and $`S_{2}`$ the final state. We assume their
supports are $`\operatorname{support}(S_{0})=\{s_{0,1},s_{0,2}\}`$,
$`\operatorname{support}(S_{1})=\{s_{1,1},s_{1,2}\}`$, and
$`\operatorname{support}(S_{2})=\{s_{2,1},s_{2,2}\}`$. The ground-truth
reasoning trajectories are defined as
$`\tau_{0}^{\star}=(s_{0,1},s_{1,1},s_{2,1})`$ and
$`\tau_{1}^{\star}=(s_{0,2},s_{1,2},s_{2,2})`$, giving the ground-truth
transition $`\bar{P}_{n}(S_{n}|S_{n-1})`$ at step $`1\leq n\leq 2`$ as

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{P}_{n}(S_{n}|S_{n-1})=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }(S_{n},S_{n-1})=(s_{n,m},s_{n-1,m})\text{ for all }n,m\in[2],\\
0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
``` |  |

We define $`P_{u,n}`$ as a uniform distribution such that

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
P_{u,n}(S_{n}|S_{n-1})=\frac{1}{2}\text{\quad if $(S_{n},S_{n-1})=(s_{n,m^{\prime}},s_{n-1,m})$}\text{\, for all $n,m,m^{\prime}\in[2]$}.
``` |  |

With these assumptions in place, we turn to the questions outlined in
Sec. [1.1](#S1.SS1 "1.1 Our Contributions ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
Regarding the first question,
Theorem [4.4](#S4.Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 4.4 (Sufficient Conditions for Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
demonstrates that conditions for the pre-trained models to bootstrap the
RL-STaR algorithm are that the pre-trained LLM captures certain critical
features of the ground-truth transition, thus enabling it to surpass a
randomly initialized model. The following theorem subsequently verifies
this condition.

###### Theorem 4.4 (Sufficient Conditions for Pre-trained Models).

Given the toy example defined in the previous paragraph, let
Assumptions [4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Assumption 4.2 (Training set). ‣ 4.2 The Family 𝑃_𝑛⁢[𝛿] and Standing Assumptions ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
and [4.3](#S4.Thmtheorem3 "Assumption 4.3 (Exact fitting). ‣ 4.2 The Family 𝑃_𝑛⁢[𝛿] and Standing Assumptions ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
hold, so that $`\mathcal{D}=\{(s_{0,1},s_{2,1}),(s_{0,2},s_{2,2})\}`$.
Assume that the pre-trained LLM estimates
$`P_{0,n}=P_{n}[\delta_{0,n}]`$
(Definition [4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Definition 4.1 (𝛿-accurate transition). ‣ 4.2 The Family 𝑃_𝑛⁢[𝛿] and Standing Assumptions ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"))
at every CoT step $`n\in[2]`$, for some $`0\leq\delta_{0,n}<1`$. If, at
the start of RL-STaR iteration $`t`$, there exist
$`0\leq\delta_{t-1,n}<1`$ with $`P_{t-1,n}=P_{n}[\delta_{t-1,n}]`$ for
every step $`n\in[2]`$, then $`P_{t,n}=P_{n}[\delta_{t,n}]`$ for every
step $`n\in[2]`$, where

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
0\leq\delta_{t,1}=\delta_{t,2}=\frac{\delta_{t-1,1}+\delta_{t-1,2}}{\delta_{t-1,1}\delta_{t-1,2}+1}<1.
``` |  |

Besides, conditions on the values of $`\delta_{0,1}`$ and
$`\delta_{0,2}`$ can be listed as follows:

1.  (a)
    If $`0<\delta_{0,1}`$ and $`0<\delta_{0,2}`$, then for all
    $`t\geq 1`$,

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \delta_{t-1,1}<\delta_{t,1}\quad\text{and}\quad\delta_{t-1,2}<\delta_{t,2}.
    ``` |  |
2.  (b)
    If exactly one of $`\delta_{0,1}`$ or $`\delta_{0,2}`$ is
    zero—meaning there exist $`n,n^{\prime}\in\{1,2\}`$ with
    $`\delta_{0,n}=0`$ but $`\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}>0`$—then

    |     |                                                             |     |
    |-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
    |     |
           ``` math
           \delta_{1,n}=\delta_{1,n^{\prime}}=\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}>0,
           ```                                                          |     |

    and for all $`t>1`$,

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \delta_{t-1,1}<\delta_{t,1}\quad\text{and}\quad\delta_{t-1,2}<\delta_{t,2}.
    ``` |  |
3.  (c)
    If both $`\delta_{0,1}=0`$ and $`\delta_{0,2}=0`$, then for all
    $`t\geq 1`$,

    |     |                              |     |
    |-----|------------------------------|-----|
    |     |
           ``` math
           \delta_{t,1}=\delta_{t,2}=0.
           ```                           |     |

###### Proof.

The proof is
in [A.2.1](#A1.SS2.SSS1 "A.2.1 Proof of Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
∎

Building upon the preceding theorem, we can establish the convergence
rate of $`\delta_{t,n}`$. This result is presented in the following
theorem

###### Theorem 4.5 (Convergence Speed of $`\delta_{t}`$).

Given the toy example defined in
Sec. [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
if $`\delta_{t,1}=\delta_{t,2}>0`$ for all $`t\geq 1`$, we define
$`\delta_{t}=\delta_{t,1}=\delta_{t,2}`$. Then,
$`\delta_{t}=\left(\left(\frac{\delta_{0}^{-1}+1}{\delta_{0}^{-1}-1}\right)^{2^{t}}-1\right)\Bigg/\left(\left(\frac{\delta_{0}^{-1}+1}{\delta_{0}^{-1}-1}\right)^{2^{t}}+1\right)`$
.

###### Proof.

The proof is
in [A.2.2](#A1.SS2.SSS2 "A.2.2 Proof of Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
∎

We also address the remaining questions about the STaR algorithm for
this toy example, as detailed in the following.

###### Corollary 4.6 (Policy Improvement in the Toy Example).

Given the toy example defined in
Sec. [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
let $`P_{t}`$ be the transition model at iteration $`t`$ of RL-STaR
training. If $`\delta_{t,1}=\delta_{t,2}>0`$ for all $`t\geq 1`$, we
define $`\delta_{t}=\delta_{t,1}=\delta_{t,2}`$. Then,

|     |                      |     |
|-----|----------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       J(P_{t})>J(P_{t-1}).
       ```                   |     |

###### Proof.

The proof is
in [A.2.3](#A1.SS2.SSS3 "A.2.3 Proof of Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
∎

###### Corollary 4.7 (Convergence to Optimal Policy in the Toy Example).

Given the toy example defined in
Sec. [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
If $`\delta_{t,1}=\delta_{t,2}>0`$ for all $`t\geq 1`$, we define
$`\delta_{t}=\delta_{t,1}=\delta_{t,2}`$. Define $`P^{\star}`$ as the
optimal estimated transition, which maximizes the reward
$`J(P^{\star})`$. This maximum is achieved when

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
J(P^{\star})=\lim_{\delta\rightarrow 1}\left(\frac{1+\delta^{2}}{2}\right)=1.
``` |  |

###### Proof.

The proof is
in [A.2.4](#A1.SS2.SSS4 "A.2.4 Proof of Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
∎

###### Corollary 4.8 (Diminishing of Incorrect Reasoning Trajectories).

Given the toy example defined in
Sec. [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
If $`\delta_{t,1}=\delta_{t,2}>0`$ for all $`t\geq 1`$, we define
$`\delta_{t}=\delta_{t,1}=\delta_{t,2}`$. Denote $`\tau^{\prime}`$ as
the incorrect reasoning trajectories included in the dataset
$`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$. There are two types of $`\tau^{\prime}`$ in this
toy example:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tau^{\prime}=(s_{0,1},s_{1,2},s_{2,1}),\quad\text{and}\quad\tau^{\prime}=(s_{0,2},s_{1,1},s_{2,2}).
``` |  |

When $`t`$ increases, the probability of $`\tau^{\prime}\in D`$
diminishes. Specifically,

|     |                                                                |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}p(\tau^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}_{t})=0.
       ```                                                             |     |

###### Proof.

The proof is
in [A.2.5](#A1.SS2.SSS5 "A.2.5 Proof of Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
∎

We move on to a more general case in the next section.

### 4.4 Main Theorem

After introducing a toy example, we now present our main theorem, which
can be applied to an arbitrary number of reasoning steps $`N`$ and an
arbitrary number of states $`M`$ for each step. In this scenario,
$`S_{0}`$ is a random variable that represents the initial state,
$`S_{1},\dots,S_{N-1}`$ represent the intermediate states of steps $`1`$
to $`N-1`$ respectively, and $`S_{N}`$ represents the final state. Each
step $`n\in[N]`$ contains $`M`$ possible states, so
$`\operatorname{support}(S_{n})=\{s_{n,1},s_{n,2},\dots,s_{n,M}\}`$.
Assuming there are $`M`$ ground-truth reasoning trajectories, we denote
these trajectories as $`\{\tau_{m}|m\in[M]\}`$ where each trajectory
$`\tau_{m}`$ has the form of $`(s_{0,m},s_{1,m},\dots,s_{N,m})`$. The
transition function for step $`n`$, denoted as
$`\bar{P}_{n}(S_{n}|S_{n-1})`$, is defined as

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{P}_{n}(S_{n}|S_{n-1})=\begin{cases}1&\text{if $(S_{n},S_{n-1})=(s_{n,m},s_{n-1,m})$}\text{ for all $m\in[M]$},\\
0&\text{if $(S_{n},S_{n-1})=(s_{n,m^{\prime}\neq m},s_{n-1,m})$ }\text{ for all $m,m^{\prime}\in[M]$},\end{cases}
``` |  |

and the uniform transition at step $`n`$, denoted as
$`P_{u,n}(S_{n}|S_{n-1})`$, is defined as

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
P_{u,n}(S_{n}|S_{n-1})=\frac{1}{M}\quad\text{for all }(S_{n},S_{n-1}).
``` |  |

We now address the questions listed in
Sec. [1.1](#S1.SS1 "1.1 Our Contributions ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
In response to the first question,
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
indicates that a condition for the pre-trained models to bootstrap the
RL-STaR algorithm is that the pre-trained LLM outperforms a randomly
initialized model at every reasoning step.

###### Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models).

Given the scenario defined in the previous paragraph, let
Assumptions [4.2](#S4.Thmtheorem2 "Assumption 4.2 (Training set). ‣ 4.2 The Family 𝑃_𝑛⁢[𝛿] and Standing Assumptions ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
and [4.3](#S4.Thmtheorem3 "Assumption 4.3 (Exact fitting). ‣ 4.2 The Family 𝑃_𝑛⁢[𝛿] and Standing Assumptions ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
hold, and assume that the pre-trained LLM estimates
$`P_{0,n}=P_{n}[\delta_{0,n}]`$ at every CoT step $`n\in[N]`$, for some
$`0\leq\delta_{0,n}<1`$. If, at the start of RL-STaR iteration $`t`$,
there exist $`0\leq\delta_{t-1,n}<1`$ with
$`P_{t-1,n}=P_{n}[\delta_{t-1,n}]`$ for every CoT step $`n\in[N]`$, then
$`P_{t,n}=P_{n}[\delta_{t,n}]`$ for all $`n\in[N]`$, where

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\delta_{t,n}=\frac{(M-2)\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{t-1,k}+\prod_{k\neq n}\delta_{t-1,k}+\delta_{t-1,n}}{(M-1)\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{t-1,k}+1}.
``` |  |

Besides, based on the values of $`\delta_{0,n}`$, we have the following
cases:

1.  (a)
    If $`0<\delta_{0,n}<1`$ for each $`n\in[N]`$, then for all
    $`t\geq 1`$,

    |     |                                |     |
    |-----|--------------------------------|-----|
    |     |
           ``` math
           \delta_{t-1,n}<\delta_{t,n}<1.
           ```                             |     |
2.  (b)
    If there exists a step $`n\in[N]`$ satisfying $`\delta_{0,n}=0`$ and
    for any other $`n^{\prime}\neq n,~n^{\prime}\in[N]`$ we have
    $`\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}>0`$, then when $`t=1`$,

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \delta_{1,n}=\prod_{n^{\prime}\neq n}\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}>0\quad\text{and}\quad\delta_{1,n^{\prime}}=\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}>0,
    ``` |  |

    and for all $`t>1`$,

    |     |                                                              |     |
    |-----|--------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
    |     |
           ``` math
           \delta_{t-1,n}<\delta_{t,n}<1.\quad\text{for all $n\in[N]$}.
           ```                                                           |     |
3.  (c)
    If there exist two distinct steps $`n,n^{\prime}\in[N]`$ such that
    $`\delta_{0,n}=0=\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}`$, then for all $`t\geq 1`$,

    |     |                                                           |     |
    |-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|
    |     |
           ``` math
           \delta_{t,n}=\delta_{t-1,n}\quad\text{for all $n\in[N]$}.
           ```                                                        |     |

###### Proof.

The proof is
in [A.2.7](#A1.SS2.SSS7 "A.2.7 Proof of Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
∎

The above theorem establishes three key points:

- [(a)](#S4.I3.i1 "Item (a) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
  If $`\delta_{0,n}>0`$ for all $`n\in[N]`$, then $`\delta_{t,n}`$ is
  strictly increasing in $`t`$.
- [(b)](#S4.I3.i2 "Item (b) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
  There can be at most one step $`n`$ with $`\delta_{0,n}=0`$. After the
  first iteration of RL-STaR, we have $`\delta_{1,n}>0`$ for all
  $`n\in[N]`$, and hence by
  [(a)](#S4.I3.i1 "Item (a) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
  $`\delta_{t,k}>0`$ will be strictly increasing in $`t`$ for all
  $`t>1`$ and $`k\in[N]`$.
- [(c)](#S4.I3.i3 "Item (c) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
  Conversely, if more than one step satisfies $`\delta_{0,n}=0`$, then
  $`\delta_{t,k}`$ remains unchanged for all $`t\geq 1`$.

In conclusion, the conditions of a pre-trained model to improve itself
through RL-STaR are to satisfy
[(a)](#S4.I3.i1 "Item (a) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
or at least
[(b)](#S4.I3.i2 "Item (b) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
The following theorem establishes the convergence speed of
$`\delta_{t,n}`$ toward $`1`$.

###### Theorem 4.10 (Convergence Speed of $`\delta_{t,n}`$).

Given the scenario defined in
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner") [(a)](#S4.I3.i1 "Item (a) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
or
[(b)](#S4.I3.i2 "Item (b) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
denote

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\gamma=\begin{cases}\frac{1-\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{0,k}}{(M-1)\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{0,k}+1}\quad\text{if~\ref{theorem:item_d1} is satisfied},\\
\frac{1-\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{1,k}}{(M-1)\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{1,k}+1}\quad\text{if~\ref{theorem:item_d2} is satisfied}.\end{cases}
``` |  |

Then for any $`\varepsilon\in\left(0,\frac{M}{N(M+1)}\right)`$, it holds
that

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\delta_{t,n}>1-\varepsilon,~`$ | $`\displaystyle\forall t\geq\left\lceil\frac{\log\frac{M+1}{M\gamma}+\log\left(N-\sum_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{0,k}\right)}{\log(1/\gamma)}\right\rceil_{+}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\quad+\left\lceil\log_{2}\left(\frac{\log M+\log\frac{1-N\varepsilon}{N\varepsilon}}{\log\frac{(M+1)-M\gamma}{\gamma}}\right)\right\rceil_{+}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\quad+\left\lfloor 1-\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{0,k}\right\rfloor_{+}\quad\text{for every $n\in[N]$}.`$ |  |

###### Proof.

The proof is
in [A.2.8](#A1.SS2.SSS8 "A.2.8 Proof of Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
∎

The remaining questions in
Sec. [1.1](#S1.SS1 "1.1 Our Contributions ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
are answered by the subsequent corollaries.

###### Corollary 4.11 (Policy Improvement).

Suppose the assumptions of
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner") [(a)](#S4.I3.i1 "Item (a) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
or
[(b)](#S4.I3.i2 "Item (b) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
hold. Let $`P_{t}=\{P_{t,n}\}_{n=1}^{N}`$ represent the estimated
transition by the model in the $`t`$-th iteration of RL-STaR training.
Then the training process improves $`J(P_{t})`$. Specifically,
$`J(P_{t+1})\geq J(P_{t})`$.

###### Proof.

The proof is
in [A.2.9](#A1.SS2.SSS9 "A.2.9 Proof of Corollary ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
∎

###### Corollary 4.12 (Convergence to the Optimal Policy).

Suppose the assumptions of
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner") [(a)](#S4.I3.i1 "Item (a) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
or
[(b)](#S4.I3.i2 "Item (b) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
hold. If the optimal transition $`P^{\star}`$ matches the $`M\times M`$
identity transition $`I_{M}`$ in every CoT step, when the training
iteration $`t`$ of RL-STaR approaches infinity,
$`P_{t}=\{P_{t,n}\}_{n=1}^{N}`$ will converge to $`P^{\star}`$. That is,
$`\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\|P_{t,n}-I_{M}\|_{\infty}=0~\text{for all}~n\in[N]`$.

###### Proof.

The proof is
in [A.2.10](#A1.SS2.SSS10 "A.2.10 Proof of Corollary ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
∎

###### Corollary 4.13 (Diminishing of Incorrect Reasoning Trajectories).

Suppose the assumptions of
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner") [(a)](#S4.I3.i1 "Item (a) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
or
[(b)](#S4.I3.i2 "Item (b) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
hold. In iterations $`t`$ of RL-STaR, denote $`\tau_{t,k}`$ to be a
trajectory containing $`k`$ incorrect reasoning steps in
$`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$. Then, the probability that RL-CoT generates
trajectories containing incorrect reasoning steps will diminish as $`t`$
increases. Specifically,
$`\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}p\left(\bigcup_{k}\tau_{t,k}\right)=0`$.

###### Proof.

The proof is
in [A.2.11](#A1.SS2.SSS11 "A.2.11 Proof of Corollary ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
∎

### 4.5 Comparison with the Convergence Analysis of Policy-Gradient Methods

At first glance, STaR ([Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib11)) might appear
to be an offline variant of policy-gradient methods in reinforcement
learning, suggesting that classical convergence guarantees ([Phansalkar
and Thathachar, 1995](#bib.bib47); [Bhandari and Russo,
2021](#bib.bib16); [Bhandari and Russo, 2024](#bib.bib22)) could be
directly applied, rendering STaR’s convergence analysis trivial.
However, to provide a clear comparison between STaR and RL-style
policy-gradient methods, we first revisit the distinguishing
characteristics of STaR’s convergence:

1.  1.
    STaR exploits the inductive biases of a pretrained LLM to bootstrap
    improved reasoning traces.
2.  2.
    The reward signal is sparse, depending solely on the final
    correctness of the answer.
3.  3.
    Iterative self-training enables progressive refinement of
    intermediate reasoning steps.

Although both STaR and policy-gradient methods can operate under similar
settings—such as receiving a reward only at the final step, or being
initialized from a pre-trained model—their training dynamics differ
fundamentally. Besides, from a theoretical perspective, the convergence
guarantees of these policy-gradient algorithms focus on the maximization
of the expected return, $`\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}[v_{t}]`$. These
guarantees ensure that the parameter $`\theta`$ converges to a local (or
global) optimum of the expected return, but do not provide assurances
about the improvement of intermediate reasoning steps. This distinction
creates different learning dynamics—STaR may gradually suppress
incorrect intermediate reasoning steps if the base model is biased
toward correct ones, even without stepwise rewards. Our analysis
formalizes this, showing how, under specific conditions, STaR can refine
reasoning paths through this iterative process.

## 5 Experiments

We conduct experiments to illustrate our theoretical analysis in
Sec. [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
For the language model, we choose GPT-2 ([Radford et al.,
2019](#bib.bib38)), Qwen2.5-0.5B ([Qwen et al., 2025](#bib.bib40)) and
Phi-3-mini ([Abdin et al., 2024](#bib.bib39)). Besides, to satisfy the
assumption of Markov property and constant state space $`M`$, we conduct
the following modifications on LLMs: For the Markov property, we
restrict the length of the context window of LLMs so that they can only
take $`s_{n-1}`$ as input when the output is $`s_{n}`$. For the
uniformity of $`\delta_{t,n}`$, we reinitialize the weights of LLMs and
pre-train them on a dataset comprising noisy trajectories whose
transitions between $`s_{n}`$ and $`s_{n-1}`$ in this dataset match the
transition probability $`P_{0}(S_{n}=s_{n}|S_{n-1}=s_{n-1})`$ referenced
in
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
For the constant $`M`$, we sample the output of LLMs within $`M`$
possible valid states for each CoT step.

Sec. [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Experiment of Theoretical and Empirical Values of 𝐽(𝑃_𝑡) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
to
Sec. [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Experiment of the Convergence of 𝐽(𝑃_𝑡) with Two 𝛿_{0,𝑛}=0 and 𝛿_{0,𝑛^′}=0 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
cover the three cases
[(a)](#S4.I3.i1 "Item (a) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")–[(c)](#S4.I3.i3 "Item (c) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
of
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner");
Sec. [5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Experiment of Non-Uniform 𝛿_{𝑡,𝑛} ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
and
Sec. [5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5 Experiment of Non-Constant 𝑀 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
then drop two of the assumptions discussed in
Sec. [6](#S6 "6 Limitations and Possible Extensions ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
For the scenario where the constant state space $`M`$ is satisfied, we
choose two reasoning tasks as shown below:

##### Task ‘zip’

This task is known as the zip operator ¹¹ 1
[https://www.w3schools.com/python/ref_func_zip.asp](https://www.w3schools.com/python/ref_func_zip.asp).
We consider the scenario with binary strings of length three. An example
of this operation is as follows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle s_{0}=\texttt{x:101,110}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\Rightarrow s_{1}=\texttt{x:10,11},\texttt{y:10}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\Rightarrow s_{2}=\texttt{x:11},\texttt{y:01,10}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\Rightarrow s_{3}=\texttt{y:11,01,10}.`$ |  |

Here, the symbols x and y represent the input and output at each step,
respectively. At each step, a single token from x is paired with the
output y. This example has total number of reasoning steps $`N=3`$, and
each step has the equal number of states $`M=64`$.

##### Task ‘dec2bin’

This is the task of converting a decimal number (that fits within three
bits) into its binary representation via long division. For example,

|     |     |                                                      |     |
|-----|-----|------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |     | $`\displaystyle s_{0}=\texttt{x:7}`$                 |     |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\Rightarrow s_{1}=\texttt{x:3,y:1}`$  |     |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\Rightarrow s_{2}=\texttt{x:1,y:11}`$ |     |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\Rightarrow s_{3}=\texttt{y:111}.`$   |     |

The process consists of three steps $`N=3`$, and each step includes
eight possible states $`M=8`$.

[TABLE]

[TABLE]

Figure 1: The first row shows the comparison of theoretical values

### 5.1 Experiment of Theoretical and Empirical Values of $`J(P_{t})`$

In this experiment, we focus on evaluating $`J(P_{t})`$ to compare its
theoretically predicted values with those observed in practice. For the
value of $`\delta_{t,n}`$, we set
$`\delta_{t,3}=\delta_{t,2}=\delta_{t,1}=\delta_{t}.`$ where
$`\delta_{t}\in\{0.1,0.2\}`$ for zip and $`\delta_{t}\in\{0.2,0.4\}`$
for dec2bin. To derive the empirical values, we train LLMs using the
training dataset $`\mathcal{D}`$ by the procedures described in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 3 Theoretical Framework ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
To derive the theoretical values, we start from
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
For the special case $`N=3`$ and $`\delta_{t,n}=\delta_{t}`$ for all
$`n`$, the value of $`\delta_{t}`$ satisfies:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\delta_{t}=\frac{(M-2)\,\delta_{t-1}^{3}+\delta_{t-1}^{2}+\delta_{t-1}}{(M-1)\,\delta_{t-1}^{3}+1}.
``` |  |

To estimate $`J(P_{t})`$, it can be shown that when $`N=3`$, a direct
calculation yields:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle J(P_{t})`$ | $`\displaystyle=e_{1}^{T}P_{t,3}P_{t,2}P_{t,1}e_{1}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\alpha_{t}^{3}+3(M-1)\alpha_{t}\beta_{t}^{2}+(M-1)(M-2)\beta_{t}^{3}`$ |  |

where $`\alpha_{t}=\frac{1+(M-1)\delta_{t}}{M}`$ and
$`\beta_{t}=\frac{1-\delta_{t}}{M}`$.

##### Results

The results are presented in
Fig. [1](#S5.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Task ‘dec2bin’ ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
In the first row, the three figures illustrate that our theoretical
model approximately matches the empirical values obtained from training
LLMs across different task settings, $`\delta_{0}`$ variations, and
model architectures. While the gap between theory and experiment differs
substantially across tasks, different LLM architectures achieve similar
empirical values. Additionally, LLMs exhibit faster convergence compared
to the theoretical predictions. This discrepancy arises because
Assumption [4.3](#S4.Thmtheorem3 "Assumption 4.3 (Exact fitting). ‣ 4.2 The Family 𝑃_𝑛⁢[𝛿] and Standing Assumptions ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
requires the transitions learned by LLMs, denoted as $`P_{t}`$, to match
the transitions in the dataset $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$ exactly. In practice,
however, this assumption is not always valid. The second-row plots
reveal a decreasing proportion of incorrect reasoning trajectories in
$`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$ as $`t`$ grows, confirming
Corollary [4.13](#S4.Thmtheorem13 "Corollary 4.13 (Diminishing of Incorrect Reasoning Trajectories). ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof. ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
that erroneous steps’ inclusion probability falls with each STaR
iteration. In the following paragraph, we discuss the cause of the
discrepancy between theoretical and empirical values.

[TABLE]

Figure 2: The comparison of transitions $`P(S_{1}|S_{0})`$, directly
extracted from dataset $`\mathcal{D}_{1}`$ (left), and the transitions
$`P_{1,1}(S_{1}|S_{0})`$ learned by LLMs during the RL-STaR algorithm
(middle). The right plot shows $`J(P_{t})`$ under different sampling
temperatures $`\mathcal{T}`$.

##### Visualization of Transition Matrix

This gap arises when LLMs put excessive probability mass on the
instances that appear more frequently in the training dataset. An
example is provided in the first two figures in
Fig. [2](#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Results ‣ 5.1 Experiment of Theoretical and Empirical Values of 𝐽(𝑃_𝑡) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
which illustrates the difference between the transitions from the
dataset and learned by GPT-2 in the task of zip when
$`\delta_{0,1}=\delta_{0,2}=\delta_{0,3}=0.22`$. The left-hand heatmap
represents the transitions directly derived from the dataset
$`\mathcal{D}_{1}`$, while the right-hand heatmap depicts the
transitions $`P_{1}`$ learned by the LLMs. Notably, the LLM-learned
transitions’ diagonal elements exhibit higher probabilities than those
in the original dataset.

##### Varying the Sampling Temperature

We also discover that this gap depends on the sampling temperature. We
varied the sampling temperature $`\mathcal{T}`$ around the default value
of $`0.5`$ to assess its influence. The last figure in
Fig. [2](#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Results ‣ 5.1 Experiment of Theoretical and Empirical Values of 𝐽(𝑃_𝑡) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
demonstrates that higher $`\mathcal{T}`$ flattens the output
distribution—slowing convergence—while lower $`\mathcal{T}`$
concentrates probability mass and speeds it up. This highlights the
importance of tuning $`\mathcal{T}`$ to strike a balance between
convergence rate and output diversity.

### 5.2 Experiment of Convergence of $`J(P_{t})`$ with One $`\delta_{0,n}=0`$

when one $`\delta_{0,n}=0`$. We apply the setting of $`\delta_{0,1}=0`$
but $`\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}=0.2`$ for $`n^{\prime}>1`$. We use GPT-2 to
perform both the zip and dec2bin tasks. However, in the dec2bin
experiment, inputs are limited to decimal numbers representable in 5
bits (i.e. $`N=5`$). All other configurations remain as detailed in
Sec. [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Experiment of Theoretical and Empirical Values of 𝐽(𝑃_𝑡) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
````
