````math
##### Results

Fig. [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Experiment of Convergence of 𝐽(𝑃_𝑡) with One 𝛿_{0,𝑛}=0 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
presents the results. In this figure, only one $`\delta_{0,n}`$ is zero,
and $`J(P_{t})`$ converges to a nearly optimal value, roughly consistent
with
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")[(b)](#S4.I3.i2 "Item (b) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
Besides $`J(P_{t})`$, we show the probability of pre-trained model
$`P_{t}`$ generating the correct transition $`(s_{n,m},s_{n-1,m})`$ for
each CoT step $`n`$, denoted by $`P_{t,n}(s_{n,m}|s_{n-1,m})`$, across
iterations $`t`$ of RL-STaR. Notably, in both tasks, the probability of
transition generated by the pre-trained model
$`P_{0,n}(s_{n,m}|s_{n-1,m})`$ does not perfectly align with the
distributions in the pre-training dataset. For instance,
$`P_{0,2}(s_{2,m}|s_{1,m})`$ is lower than $`P_{0,3}(s_{3,m}|s_{2,m})`$
even though $`\delta_{0,2}`$ and $`\delta_{0,3}`$ share the same value
in the pre-training dataset. Moreover, under the condition of
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")[(b)](#S4.I3.i2 "Item (b) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
the values of $`P_{t,2}(s_{2,m}|s_{1,m})`$ and
$`P_{t,3}(s_{3,m}|s_{2,m})`$ should remain unchanged between $`t=0`$ and
$`t=1`$. In practice, however, they increase on the first iteration.
These differences reflect the discrepancy between the theoretical and
empirical values observed in the previous experiment.

### 5.3 Experiment of the Convergence of $`J(P_{t})`$ with Two $`\delta_{0,n}=0`$ and $`\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}=0`$

In this experiment, we examine the convergence behavior of $`J(P_{t})`$
when two $`\delta_{0,n}=0`$ and $`\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}=0`$. We apply
the setting of $`\delta_{0,1}=\delta_{0,2}=0`$ but
$`\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}=0.2`$ for $`n^{\prime}>2`$. We use GPT-2 to
perform both the zip and dec2bin tasks. All other configurations remain
as detailed in
Sec. [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Experiment of Convergence of 𝐽(𝑃_𝑡) with One 𝛿_{0,𝑛}=0 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").

##### Results

Fig. [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 Experiment of Convergence of 𝐽(𝑃_𝑡) with One 𝛿_{0,𝑛}=0 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
shows that when $`\delta_{0,1}=\delta_{0,2}=0`$, $`J(P_{t})`$ fails to
converge to its near-optimal value, in agreement with
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")[(c)](#S4.I3.i3 "Item (c) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
Besides $`J(P_{t})`$, we also plot
$`P_{t,n}\bigl(s_{n,m}\mid s_{n-1,m}\bigr)`$ —the probability that the
pre-trained policy $`P_{t}`$ correctly generates the transition
$`(s_{n,m},s_{n-1,m})`$ at each CoT step $`n`$—over RL-STaR iterations
$`t`$. Although
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")[(c)](#S4.I3.i3 "Item (c) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
predicts that all $`\delta_{t,n}`$ remain constant (implying both
$`J(P_{t})`$ and each $`P_{t,n}`$ should be invariant in $`t`$), the
empirical curves for both tasks show that if $`\delta_{0,n}>0`$, then
$`P_{t,n}(s_{n,m}\mid s_{n-1,m})`$ can still approach 1, causing
$`J(P_{t})`$ to increase. The cause is the one identified in
Sec. [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Experiment of Theoretical and Empirical Values of 𝐽(𝑃_𝑡) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"):
$`P_{t,n}`$ does not reproduce $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$ exactly, but puts
extra probability mass on the transitions that occur most often in
$`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$. This lifts $`\delta_{t,n}`$ at the steps where
$`\delta_{0,n}>0`$, whereas
Assumption [4.3](#S4.Thmtheorem3 "Assumption 4.3 (Exact fitting). ‣ 4.2 The Family 𝑃_𝑛⁢[𝛿] and Standing Assumptions ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
requires exact matching, so
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")[(c)](#S4.I3.i3 "Item (c) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
predicts no change.

### 5.4 Experiment of Non-Uniform $`\delta_{t,n}`$

In this experiment, we follow the setup in
Sec. [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Experiment of Theoretical and Empirical Values of 𝐽(𝑃_𝑡) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
but for uniform case we choose $`\delta_{0,n}\in\{0.1,0.2,0.3\}`$ for
all $`n\in[N].`$ For the non-uniform case, each off-diagonal transition
$`(s_{n-1,m},s_{n,m^{\prime}})`$, $`m^{\prime}\neq m`$, uses

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\delta_{0,n,m,m^{\prime}}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[\delta_{0,n},2\delta_{0,n}],
``` |  |

ensuring $`\delta_{0,n}=\min_{m,m^{\prime}}\delta_{0,n,m,m^{\prime}}`$.

##### Results

Fig. [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 5.2 Experiment of Convergence of 𝐽(𝑃_𝑡) with One 𝛿_{0,𝑛}=0 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
shows that $`J(P_{t})`$ converges faster under non-uniform
$`\delta_{0}`$ than both the empirical and theoretical uniform-case
curves for $`\delta_{0}=\{0.1,0.2,0.3\}`$. Thus, the uniform-case
convergence rate provides a valid lower bound for the non-uniform
scenario.

### 5.5 Experiment of Non-Constant $`M`$

In this experiment, we follow the setup in
Sec. [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Experiment of Theoretical and Empirical Values of 𝐽(𝑃_𝑡) ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
but use different tasks. We choose $`\delta_{0}=\{0.2,0.3\}`$ for these
tasks. To have different number of states at each step, we use the
following task.

##### Task ‘binadd-non-const-M’

This task is a task of binary addition.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle s_{0}=\texttt{x:101+110}`$ | $`\displaystyle\Rightarrow s_{1}=\texttt{x:10+11},\texttt{z:0},\texttt{y:1}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\Rightarrow s_{2}=\texttt{x:1+1},\texttt{z:0},\texttt{y:11}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\Rightarrow s_{3}=\texttt{y:1011}.`$ |  |

The input consists of two binary numbers $`x=101,110`$. In the first
step, the last digit $`1,1`$ produces a carry $`z=0`$ and a sum $`y=1`$.
In the second step, the second digit $`0,1`$ and carry $`z=0`$ yield a
new $`z=0`$ and the result of the second digit $`y=11`$, continuing in
this manner until the final step results in $`y=1011`$. It can be shown
that $`M_{0}=64,M_{1}=48,M_{2}=28,M_{3}=15`$.

##### Task ‘binadd-const-M’

This task is a task of binary addition, but with constant $`M`$. We
create this task by concatenating $`s_{0}`$ to $`s_{1},s_{2}`$ and
$`s_{3}`$, as follows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle s_{0}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\texttt{x:101+110}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\Rightarrow s_{1}=\texttt{x:101+110,x:10+11},\texttt{z:0},\texttt{y:1}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\Rightarrow s_{2}=\texttt{x:101+110,x:1+1},\texttt{z:0},\texttt{y:11}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\Rightarrow s_{3}=\texttt{x:101+110,y:1011}.`$ |  |

We compare the convergence of $`J(P_{t})`$ between these two tasks, and
verify whether the task binadd-const-M can be an approximator of the
task binadd-non-const-M.

##### Results

In
Fig. [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 5.2 Experiment of Convergence of 𝐽(𝑃_𝑡) with One 𝛿_{0,𝑛}=0 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
we observe that the convergence curve $`J(P_{t})`$ in the case of
non-constant-M can be approximated by the $`J(P_{t})`$ of constant-M in
both empirical values and theoretical values. This validates our
hypothesis that the modified case can be an approximator.

## 6 Limitations and Possible Extensions

While our theorem provides useful theoretical guarantees, it also has
limitations when applied to real-world LLM settings. These limitations
include the Markov assumption of state transitions, the uniformity of
$`\delta_{t,n}`$, and the fixed state count $`M`$. Below, we discuss
these restrictions and outline how our framework could be extended to
better align with practical LLM behavior.

### 6.1 Markov Assumption of State Transitions

We simplify our analysis by modeling the reasoning process as Markovian,
even though this assumption may not strictly hold for real-world LLMs,
whose context windows can span the entire trajectory and thus violate
Markov independence. In this section, we first show that the Markov
assumption is essential for filtering out incorrect reasoning steps, and
we discuss how practical LLMs can approximate this behavior.

##### Toy Example without Markov Assumption

Suppose the pre-trained transition at step $`2`$ of the toy example in
Sec. [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
reads both $`S_{1}`$ and $`S_{0}`$ instead of $`S_{1}`$ alone. Working
through one iteration of
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 3 Theoretical Framework ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
(Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Toy Example without the Markov Assumption ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")),
the transition $`P_{1,2}`$ learned in the first iteration is already
deterministic, so
$`\mathcal{D}_{T}=\mathcal{D}_{T-1}=\cdots=\mathcal{D}_{1}`$.
Trajectories of the form
$`\tau=(s_{0,m},s_{1,m^{\prime}\neq m},s_{2,m})`$, which contain an
incorrect reasoning step, therefore stay in the dataset at every
iteration and RL-STaR cannot remove them.

##### How Real-world LLMs Approximate Markov Property

Although real-world Chain-of-Thought trajectories include the entire
context $`(S_{0},S_{1},\dots,S_{n})`$, predicting $`S_{n+1}`$ typically
relies only on a few recent steps. Several studies (e.g., ([Yao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib43); [Teng et al., 2025](#bib.bib44); [Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41); [Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib42); [Xiao and Liu,
2024](#bib.bib4); [Prystawski et al., 2024](#bib.bib3))) demonstrate
that CoT generalization stems from decomposing complex tasks into
simpler, reusable subtasks. Each subtask’s outcome depends on a limited
window of prior reasoning steps, so the training data effectively
exhibits a Markovian structure. Consequently, when LLMs focus on these
local dependencies and ignore unnecessary earlier context, they
approximate the Markov property in practice.

### 6.2 Uniformity of $`\delta_{t,n}`$

We assume that $`\delta_{0,n}`$ is uniform across all states at step
$`n`$, but real pre-trained LLMs rarely satisfy this idealization.
Allowing $`\delta_{0,n,m,m^{\prime}}`$ for each transition from
$`s_{n-1,m}`$ to $`s_{n,m^{\prime}}`$ to take various values complicates
the analysis substantially. However, we will show that it is possible to
extend our theorem to non-uniform cases.

##### Non-Uniform $`\delta_{0,n}`$

In this section, we show that even though our theorem does not directly
apply, we can still derive a valid lower bound by comparing the
original, non-uniform transition $`P_{0,n}`$ to a worst-case uniform
model $`\underline{P}_{0,n}`$. We begin by defining

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{cases}P_{0,n}\bigl(S_{n}=s_{n,m^{\prime}}\mid S_{n-1}=s_{n-1,m}\bigr)=\frac{1-\delta_{0,n,m,m^{\prime}}}{M}\text{for all $m^{\prime}\neq m$, and $m,m^{\prime}\in[M]$,}\\
P_{0,n}\bigl(S_{n}=s_{n,m}\mid S_{n-1}=s_{n-1,m}\bigr)=\frac{1+\sum_{m^{\prime}\in[M]~\text{and}~m^{\prime}\neq m}\delta_{0,n,m,m^{\prime}}}{M}.\end{cases}
``` |  |

Let
$`\underline{\delta}_{0,n}=\min_{m,m^{\prime}\in[M]}\delta_{0,n,m,m^{\prime}}`$,
and define a uniform transition

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{cases}\underline{P}_{0,n}\bigl(S_{n}=s_{n,m^{\prime}}\mid S_{n-1}=s_{n-1,m}\bigr)=\frac{1-\underline{\delta}_{0,n}}{M}\quad\text{for all $m^{\prime}\neq m$, and $m,m^{\prime}\in[M]$},\\
\underline{P}_{0,n}\bigl(S_{n}=s_{n,m}\mid S_{n-1}=s_{n-1,m}\bigr)=\frac{1+(M-1)\,\underline{\delta}_{0,n}}{M}.\end{cases}
``` |  |

By construction, $`\underline{P}_{0,n}`$ is no more accurate than
$`P_{0,n}`$ at selecting the correct step but does satisfy the
uniform-$`\delta`$ condition. Applying
Theorem [4.10](#S4.Thmtheorem10 "Theorem 4.10 (Convergence Speed of 𝛿_{𝑡,𝑛}). ‣ Proof. ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
to $`\underline{P}_{0,n}`$ gives the convergence rate of
$`\delta_{t,n}`$ under uniform transitions, which therefore serves as a
lower bound on the convergence speed for the original, non-uniform case.
We validate this lower bound with the experimental results shown in
Sec. [5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Experiment of Non-Uniform 𝛿_{𝑡,𝑛} ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").

### 6.3 Fixed Number of States $`M`$

In our framework, each reasoning step is assumed to take one of $`M`$
possible states. While this finite-state assumption is common in
theoretical analyses of Chain-of-Thought reasoning (e.g., ([Xiao and
Liu, 2024](#bib.bib4); [Feng et al., 2024](#bib.bib5); [Yao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib43); [Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib41))), it does not always
hold in practice. Large language models can freely generate arbitrary
strings rather than being confined to a fixed state set. Even if the
model’s outputs are drawn from a bounded vocabulary, the effective
number of states available at each step may still vary substantially.

##### LLMs Generate Arbitrary Strings

In real-world deployments, LLMs can emit any text, not just tokens from
a fixed set. For example, in an arithmetic task, the model might output
Python code instead of a numerical expression. A plausible solution for
this scenario is to introduce an extra state $`s^{\prime}`$ that
represents all out-of-set outputs and redefine the state count as
$`M^{\prime}=M+1`$. However, since $`s^{\prime}`$ does not lead to a
valid terminal state, it complicates convergence and correctness
guarantees. Extending the theoretical framework to accommodate this
setting is an interesting direction for future work.

##### Different Number of States at Each Reasoning Step

Some reasoning tasks may feature a different number of candidate states
at each step. Let $`M_{n}`$ denote the number of states at step
$`n\in[N]`$. We consider two scenarios:

- •
  $`M_{n}`$ is nonincreasing: $`M_{0}\geq M_{1}\geq\cdots\geq M_{N}.`$
- •
  There exist indices $`n<n^{\prime}`$ such that
  $`M_{n}<M_{n^{\prime}}`$.

First, we focus on the first scenario. In this setting, we reformulate
the problem by creating composite states: each state in the step $`n`$
of ground-truth trajectory as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle s_{n,m_{n}}\,\in\,\operatorname{support}(S_{n}),\text{where}~|\operatorname{support}(S_{n})|=M_{n},~\text{and}~m_{n}\in[M_{n}],`$ |  |

is paired with its initial state $`s_{0,m_{0}}`$ to form a new state
$`\bigl(s_{0,m_{0}},\,s_{n,m_{n}}\bigr).`$ This construction is
illustrated in the diagram below:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,) |  |

Before concatenation, step 0 has $`M_{0}`$ states and step $`n`$ has
$`M_{n}`$. After concatenation, each composite state
$`(s_{0,m_{0}},s_{n,m_{n}})`$ yields exactly $`M_{0}`$ states at step
$`n`$, so we set $`M=M_{0}`$ for all $`n`$. By applying
Theorem [4.10](#S4.Thmtheorem10 "Theorem 4.10 (Convergence Speed of 𝛿_{𝑡,𝑛}). ‣ Proof. ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
to this constant-$`M`$ setting, we obtain a convergence rate that we
conjecture approximates that of the original varying-$`M`$ problem. In
Sec. [5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5 Experiment of Non-Constant 𝑀 ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
we empirically compare this approximated rate with the convergence
behavior observed in the original task. However, owing to the challenges
of analyzing the non-constant $`M`$ case, we present only empirical
results and leave the theoretical analysis as future work.

For the second scenario, the ground-truth reasoning paths form a DAG. In
this case, one state at step $`n`$ leads to multiple ground-truth
transitions with non-zero probability at step $`n+1`$, which complicates
the analysis. However, to illustrate how our framework can handle
certain forms of trajectory multiplicity, consider the case where
multiple correct intermediate steps exist but ultimately converge to the
same final answer. For instance, suppose we are given two input
questions, $`s_{0,0}=1+2+3`$ and $`s_{0,1}=2+3+4`$, each with multiple
valid reasoning paths leading to their respective correct answers. In
the following, we show that these intermediate trajectories can be
merged into single abstract states $`s_{1,0}`$ and $`s_{1,1}`$, allowing
our framework to operate over equivalence classes of states. In this
example, we define the ground-truth reasoning steps and final answers as
follows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle s_{0,0}=1+2+3\Rightarrow s_{1,0,0}=3+3\Rightarrow s_{2,0}=6`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle s_{0,0}=1+2+3\Rightarrow s_{1,0,1}=1+5\Rightarrow s_{2,0}=6`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle s_{0,1}=2+3+4\Rightarrow s_{1,1,0}=5+4\Rightarrow s_{2,1}=9`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle s_{0,1}=2+3+4\Rightarrow s_{1,1,1}=2+7\Rightarrow s_{2,1}=9`$ |  |

And the transition probability is as follows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle P(S_{1}|S_{0})=\begin{cases}\frac{1+\delta_{2}}{4}&\text{if $S_{1}\in\{s_{1,m,0},s_{1,m,1}\}$ and $S_{0}=s_{0,m}$},\\
\frac{1+\delta_{2}}{4}&\text{if $S_{1}\in\{s_{1,m,0},s_{1,m,1}\}$ and $S_{0}=s_{0,m^{\prime}\neq m}$},\\
\end{cases}`$ |  |

and

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle P(S_{2}|S_{1})=\begin{cases}\frac{1+\delta_{1}}{2}&\text{if $S_{2}=s_{2,m}$ and $S_{1}\in\{s_{1,m,0},s_{1,m,1}\}$},\\
\frac{1+\delta_{1}}{2}&\text{if $S_{2}=s_{2,m^{\prime}\neq m}$ and $S_{1}\in\{s_{1,m,0},s_{1,m,1}\}$}.\\
\end{cases}`$ |  |

In the above case, we can merge $`s_{1,1,0},s_{1,1,1}`$ into $`s_{1,1}`$
and $`s_{1,0,0},s_{1,0,1}`$ into $`s_{1,0}`$, and the ground-truth
trajectories with merged states become:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle s_{0,0}=1+2+3\Rightarrow s_{1,0}=(3+3,1+5)\Rightarrow s_{2,0}=6`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle s_{0,1}=2+3+4\Rightarrow s_{1,1}=(5+4,2+7)\Rightarrow s_{2,1}=9`$ |  |

And the transition probability becomes:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle P(S_{1}|S_{0})=\begin{cases}\frac{1+2\delta_{2}}{2}&\text{if $S_{1}=s_{1,m}$ and $S_{0}=s_{0,m}$}\\
\frac{1+2\delta_{2}}{2}&\text{if $S_{1}=s_{1,m}$ and $S_{0}=s_{0,m^{\prime}\neq m}$}\\
\end{cases}`$ |  |

and

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle P(S_{2}|S_{1})=\begin{cases}\frac{1+\delta_{1}}{2}&\text{if $S_{2}=s_{2,m}$ and $S_{1}=s_{1,m}$}\\
\frac{1+\delta_{1}}{2}&\text{if $S_{2}=s_{2,m^{\prime}\neq m}$ and $S_{1}=s_{1,m}$}\\
\end{cases}`$ |  |

This setting can still be accommodated within our framework. However,
when the ground-truth trajectories differ in their number of reasoning
steps $`N`$—for instance, when certain solution paths omit intermediate
steps—our current analysis no longer applies directly. Such scenarios
are more complex to handle and are left for future work.

## 7 Conclusion

We propose RL-STaR, a theoretical framework for analyzing the core
properties of the Self-Taught Reasoner (STaR) algorithm. Assuming
suitably bootstrapped pre-trained models, we prove that RL-STaR yields
policy improvement and converges toward the optimal policy—even when the
training data include erroneous reasoning trajectories. Although our
analysis abstracts away many complexities of real-world LLM deployments,
it offers a rigorous account of why STaR works and lays the groundwork
for extending this theory to more realistic settings in future work.

## Appendix A Appendix

### A.1 Additional Notation

The proofs in this appendix use the following notation in addition to
that of
Sec. [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Notations ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").

- •
  $`(s_{i},s_{k})\Subset\tau`$: the elements $`s_{i}`$ and $`s_{k}`$
  both occur in the tuple $`\tau=(s_{i},s_{j},\dots,s_{k},s_{l})`$, with
  $`s_{i}`$ preceding $`s_{k}`$.
- •
  $`\mathbb{I}\{a=b\}`$: $`\mathbb{I}\{a=b\}=1`$ if $`a=b`$; otherwise
  $`\mathbb{I}\{a=b\}=0`$.
- •
  $`\mathbf{1}`$: the all-ones vector.

### A.2 Proof of Theorems

#### A.2.1 Proof of Theorem [4.4](#S4.Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 4.4 (Sufficient Conditions for Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")

###### Proof.

Without loss of generality, we prove the case when $`t=1`$. This is the
case of the first iteration of RL-STaR Algorithm. First, we illustrate
the transition probability of the pre-trained LLM $`P_{0,n}`$ as shown
in
Fig. [7](#A1.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Proof. ‣ A.2.1 Proof of Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 7: Transition probabilities of the pre-trained LLM $`P_{0,n}`$ in
the toy example used in the proof of
Theorem [4.4](#S4.Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 4.4 (Sufficient Conditions for Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").

To begin with, we have an equal probability of selecting either sample
$`(s_{0,1},s_{2,1})`$ or $`(s_{0,2},s_{2,2})`$ from $`\mathcal{D}`$.
Consequently, we obtain the trajectories $`\tau`$ from the above
transition for $`m\in\{1,2\}`$, with the following probabilities

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p(\tau)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1+\delta_{0,1}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1+\delta_{0,2}}{2}\right)&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,1},s_{1,1},s_{2,1}),\\
\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1+\delta_{0,1}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1-\delta_{0,2}}{2}\right)&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,1},s_{1,1},s_{2,2}),\\
\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1-\delta_{0,1}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1-\delta_{0,2}}{2}\right)&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,1},s_{1,2},s_{2,1}),\\
\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1-\delta_{0,1}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1+\delta_{0,2}}{2}\right)&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,1},s_{1,2},s_{2,2}),\\
\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1-\delta_{0,1}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1+\delta_{0,2}}{2}\right)&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,2},s_{1,1},s_{2,1}),\\
\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1-\delta_{0,1}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1-\delta_{0,2}}{2}\right)&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,2},s_{1,1},s_{2,2}),\\
\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1+\delta_{0,1}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1-\delta_{0,2}}{2}\right)&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,2},s_{1,2},s_{2,1}),\\
\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1+\delta_{0,1}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1+\delta_{0,2}}{2}\right)&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,2},s_{1,2},s_{2,2}),\\
\end{cases}
``` |  | (1) |

where $`m,n\in[2]`$ and $`m\neq m^{\prime}`$. In the first iteration of
the RL-STaR algorithm, the trajectories $`\tau`$ that satisfy
$`(s_{0,m},s_{2,m})\Subset\tau`$ can be exclusively collected in the
dataset $`\mathcal{D}_{1}`$. Therefore, the conditional probability for
$`\tau`$ such that $`\tau\in\mathcal{D}_{1}`$ is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p(\tau|\tau\in\mathcal{D}_{1})=\begin{cases}\frac{(1+\delta_{0,1})(1+\delta_{0,2})}{4(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,1},s_{1,1},s_{2,1}),\\
\frac{(1-\delta_{0,1})(1-\delta_{0,2})}{4(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,1},s_{1,2},s_{2,1}),\\
\frac{(1-\delta_{0,1})(1-\delta_{0,2})}{4(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,2},s_{1,1},s_{2,2}),\\
\frac{(1+\delta_{0,1})(1+\delta_{0,2})}{4(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,2},s_{1,2},s_{2,2}).\\
\end{cases}
``` |  | (2) |

Based on this dataset, we assume that the LLMs can perfectly learn the
conditional transition $`P(S_{n+1,m}|S_{n,m})`$ based on the
probabilities of $`(s_{n,m},s_{n+1,m})\Subset\tau`$ and
$`(s_{n,m},s_{n+1,m^{\prime}\neq m})\Subset\tau`$ from the
$`\tau\sim p(\tau|\tau\in\mathcal{D}_{1})`$. For example,
$`P(S_{1,1}|s_{0,1})`$ can be obtained from

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle P(s_{1,1}|s_{0,1})`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{p((s_{0,1},s_{1,1})\Subset\tau|\tau\in\mathcal{D}_{1})}{\sum_{j\in[2]}p((s_{0,1},s_{1,j})\Subset\tau|\tau\in\mathcal{D}_{1})}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\frac{(1+\delta_{0,1})(1+\delta_{0,2})}{4(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}}{\frac{(1+\delta_{0,1})(1+\delta_{0,2})}{4(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}+\frac{(1-\delta_{0,1})(1-\delta_{0,2})}{4(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{(1+\delta_{0,1})(1+\delta_{0,2})}{2(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}.`$ |  |

Hence, the transition $`P_{1}`$ is

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
P_{1}(S_{n}|S_{n-1})=\begin{cases}\frac{(1+\delta_{0,1})(1+\delta_{0,2})}{2(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}\\
\quad\text{if $S_{n-1}=s_{n-1,m}$, $S_{n}=s_{n,m}$,}\\
\frac{(1-\delta_{0,1})(1-\delta_{0,2})}{2(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}\\
\quad\text{if $S_{n-1}=s_{n-1,m}$, $S_{n}=s_{n,m^{\prime}\neq m}$,}\end{cases}
``` |  |

for all $`n,m,m^{\prime}\in[2]`$, which can be illustrated as in
Fig. [8](#A1.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Proof. ‣ A.2.1 Proof of Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 8: Transition probabilities $`P_{1}`$ after the first iteration
of RL-STaR in the toy example used in the proof of
Theorem [4.4](#S4.Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 4.4 (Sufficient Conditions for Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").

If RL-STaR improves the transition probabilities in each iteration, then
the probabilities of transitions matching the ground-truth trajectories
will increase. Specifically, we have
$`P_{1}(S_{n}=s_{n,m}|S_{n-1}=s_{n-1,m})>P_{1}(S_{n}=s_{n,m^{\prime}\neq m}|S_{n-1}=s_{n-1,m})`$.
Now we need to prove that

|     |                                |     |
|-----|--------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \delta_{t-1,m}<\delta_{t,m}<1.
       ```                             |     |

We can get
$`\delta_{1,1}=\frac{\delta_{0,1}+\delta_{0,2}}{1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2}}`$
by

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |   $`\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \frac{(1+\delta_{0,1})(1+\delta_{0,2})}{2(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}&=\frac{(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})+\big((1+\delta_{0,1})(1+\delta_{0,2})-(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})\big)}{2(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}\\
&=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{(1+\delta_{0,1})(1+\delta_{0,2})-(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}{2(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}\\
&=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\delta_{0,1}+\delta_{0,2}}{2(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\delta_{1,1}}{2}.\end{aligned}`$ |  |

We can also show that $`\delta_{1,1}<1`$, since

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\delta_{1,1}-1`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\delta_{0,1}+\delta_{0,2}}{1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2}}-1`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{(\delta_{0,1}+\delta_{0,2})-(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}{1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2}}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{-(\delta_{0,1}-1)(\delta_{0,2}-1)}{1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2}}<0.`$ |  |

Besides, it is straightforward that the above analysis is true if we
replace $`\delta_{0,1}`$ by $`\delta_{t-1,1}`$, or replace
$`\delta_{t-1,1}`$ by $`\delta_{t-1,2}`$.

Now we consider the three conditions on the values of $`\delta_{0,1}`$
and $`\delta_{0,2}`$ as follows.

1.  (a)
    If both $`\delta_{0,1}>0`$ and $`\delta_{0,2}>0`$, we claim
    $`\delta_{1,1}-\delta_{0,1}>0`$. Indeed,

    |  |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|----|
    |  | $`\displaystyle\delta_{1,1}-\delta_{0,1}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\delta_{0,1}+\delta_{0,2}}{1+\delta_{0,1}\,\delta_{0,2}}\;-\;\delta_{0,1}`$ |  |
    |  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\delta_{0,1}+\delta_{0,2}}{1+\delta_{0,1}\,\delta_{0,2}}\;-\;\frac{\delta_{0,1}\bigl(1+\delta_{0,1}\,\delta_{0,2}\bigr)}{1+\delta_{0,1}\,\delta_{0,2}}`$ |  |
    |  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\delta_{0,2}\,\bigl(1-\delta_{0,1}^{2}\bigr)}{1+\delta_{0,1}\,\delta_{0,2}}\;>\;0,`$ |  |

    because $`\delta_{0,1},\delta_{0,2}>0`$ and $`1-\delta_{0,1}^{2}>0`$
    (note that $`\delta_{0,1}<1`$). A similar argument holds for
    $`\delta_{1,2}-\delta_{0,2}`$, ensuring
    $`\delta_{1,2}>\delta_{0,2}`$ whenever $`\delta_{0,1}>0`$ and
    $`\delta_{0,2}>0`$.
2.  (b)
    If exactly one of $`\delta_{0,1}`$ or $`\delta_{0,2}`$ is zero, we
    write $`\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}>0`$ and $`\delta_{0,n}=0`$. Then,

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \delta_{1,1}\;=\;\delta_{1,2}\;=\;\frac{0+\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}}{0+1}\;=\;\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}\;>\;0.
    ``` |  |

    Thus, starting from $`t=1`$, both $`\delta_{1,1}`$ and
    $`\delta_{1,2}`$ are strictly positive, reducing this scenario to
    the first case above for all subsequent iterations that
    $`\delta_{t,1}>0`$ and $`\delta_{t,2}>0`$.
3.  (c)
    If both $`\delta_{0,1}=0`$ and $`\delta_{0,2}=0`$, then

    |     |                                                          |     |
    |-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|
    |     |
           ``` math
           \delta_{t,1}\;=\;\delta_{t,2}\;=\;\frac{0+0}{0+1}\;=\;0,
           ```                                                       |     |

    for all $`t>0`$. In other words, once both $`\delta_{0,1}`$ and
    $`\delta_{0,2}`$ are zero, they remain zero for every iteration
    $`t`$.

∎

#### A.2.2 Proof of Theorem [4.5](#S4.Thmtheorem5 "Theorem 4.5 (Convergence Speed of 𝛿_𝑡). ‣ Proof. ‣ 4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")

###### Proof.

Let $`f(x)=\frac{2x}{1+x^{2}}`$. Using Taylor’s theorem to expand about
$`x=1`$, one has

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
f(\delta_{t})-1=f^{\prime}(1)(\delta_{t}-1)+\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(1)}{2!}(\delta_{t}-1)^{2}+\frac{f^{(3)}(\xi_{t})}{3!}(\delta_{t}-1)^{3},
``` |  |

for each $`t\geq 0`$ and some $`\xi_{t}\in(\delta_{t},1)`$. It’s
straightforward to see that $`f^{\prime}(1)=0`$,
$`f^{\prime\prime}(1)=-1`$ and
$`f^{(3)}(x)=-\frac{12\left(x^{4}-6x^{2}+1\right)}{\left(x^{2}+1\right)^{4}}`$.
Hence,

|     |                                                                   |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{|\delta_{t+1}-1|}{|\delta_{t}-1|^{2}}=0.5,
       ```                                                                |     |

which shows quadratic convergence.
To find its closed-form expression, put $`x_{t}=\delta_{t}^{-1}`$ and
rewrite our recurrence as $`x_{t+1}=({1+x_{t}^{2}})/{2x_{t}}.`$ Observe
that

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle x_{t+1}+1=\frac{(x_{t}+1)^{2}}{2x_{t}},\quad\text{and}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle x_{t+1}-1=\frac{(x_{t}-1)^{2}}{2x_{t}}.`$ |  |

One now sees that

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\frac{x_{t}+1}{x_{t}-1}=\left(\frac{x_{0}+1}{x_{0}-1}\right)^{2^{t}}.
``` |  |

Directly solving for $`x_{t}`$ and $`\delta_{t}`$, we obtain

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
x_{t}=\frac{\left(\frac{x_{0}+1}{x_{0}-1}\right)^{2^{t}}+1}{\left(\frac{x_{0}+1}{x_{0}-1}\right)^{2^{t}}-1}\quad{\text{and}}\quad\delta_{t}=\frac{\left(\frac{\delta_{0}^{-1}+1}{\delta_{0}^{-1}-1}\right)^{2^{t}}-1}{\left(\frac{\delta_{0}^{-1}+1}{\delta_{0}^{-1}-1}\right)^{2^{t}}+1}.
``` |  |

∎

#### A.2.3 Proof of Theorem [4.6](#S4.Thmtheorem6 "Corollary 4.6 (Policy Improvement in the Toy Example). ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof. ‣ 4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")

###### Proof.

From
Eq. ([1](#A1.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ Proof. ‣ A.2.1 Proof of Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")),
the reward $`J(P_{0})`$ is the probability that $`p(\tau)`$ satisfies
$`(s_{0,m},s_{2,m})\Subset\tau`$. Hence,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle J(P_{0})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1+\delta_{0,1}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1+\delta_{0,2}}{2}\right)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\quad+\left(\frac{1-\delta_{0,1}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1-\delta_{0,2}}{2}\right)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1+\delta_{0,1}\,\delta_{0,2}}{2}.`$ |  |

This expression remains valid for all $`t\geq 0`$. Moreover, since
$`\delta_{t}=\delta_{t,1}=\delta_{t,2}`$ when $`t\geq 1`$, it is obvious
that $`J(P_{t})`$ is an increasing function. Therefore,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
J(P_{t})\;=\;\frac{1+\delta_{t}^{2}}{2}\;>\;\frac{1+\delta_{t-1}^{2}}{2}\;=\;J(P_{t-1}),\quad\text{ for all $t\geq 1$},
``` |  |

which completes the proof. ∎

#### A.2.4 Proof of Theorem [4.7](#S4.Thmtheorem7 "Corollary 4.7 (Convergence to Optimal Policy in the Toy Example). ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof. ‣ 4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")

###### Proof.

We need to show that, for any $`0<\delta_{t}<1`$, the limit of
$`\delta_{t}`$ approaches $`1`$ as $`t`$ tends to infinity. Since
$`0<\delta_{t}<1`$, we have
$`(\delta_{0}^{-1}+1)\big/(\delta_{0}^{-1}-1)>1`$. It is straightforward
that by applying
Theorem [4.5](#S4.Thmtheorem5 "Theorem 4.5 (Convergence Speed of 𝛿_𝑡). ‣ Proof. ‣ 4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\delta_{t}=\frac{\left(\frac{\delta_{0}^{-1}+1}{\delta_{0}^{-1}-1}\right)^{2^{t}}-1}{\left(\frac{\delta_{0}^{-1}+1}{\delta_{0}^{-1}-1}\right)^{2^{t}}+1}=1.
``` |  |

∎

#### A.2.5 Proof of Theorem [4.8](#S4.Thmtheorem8 "Corollary 4.8 (Diminishing of Incorrect Reasoning Trajectories). ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof. ‣ 4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")

###### Proof.

Note that $`\delta_{t}=\delta_{t,1}=\delta_{t,2}`$ when $`t\geq 1`$.
Apply
Eq.([2](#A1.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ Proof. ‣ A.2.1 Proof of Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"))
and we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p(\tau^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}_{t})=\frac{(1-\delta_{t})^{2}}{4(1+\delta_{t}^{2})},
``` |  | (3) |

if $`\tau=(s_{0,1},s_{1,2},s_{2,1})`$ or
$`\tau=(s_{0,2},s_{1,1},s_{2,2})`$. We complete the proof by applying
Theorem [4.5](#S4.Thmtheorem5 "Theorem 4.5 (Convergence Speed of 𝛿_𝑡). ‣ Proof. ‣ 4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
∎

#### A.2.6 Propositions for Proving the Main Theorem

###### Proposition A.1.

Consider a non-homogeneous Markov sequence
$`S=\left(S_{n}\right)_{n=0}^{N}`$ with state space $`\mathcal{S}=[M]`$,
initial distribution $`\mu`$, and transition matrices
$`P_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times M}`$. More specifically, for each
$`n\in[N]`$

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
S_{0}\sim\mu,\quad\left[P_{n}\right]_{i,j}=P\left[S_{n}=j\mid S_{n-1}=i\right].
``` |  |

Denote by
$`\mathcal{C}=\left\{\left(s_{n}\right)_{n=0}^{N}\in\mathcal{S}^{N+1}:{s_{0}=s_{N}}\right\}`$
the set of correct trajectories, let $`\mu_{i}=\mu(\{i\})`$, and

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |   $`\displaystyle\begin{aligned} {\big[\tilde{P}_{n}\big]_{i,j}}&=P\left[S_{n}=j\mid S\in\mathcal{C},S_{n-1}=i\right]\\
&=\frac{\sum_{m=1}^{M}P\left[S_{0}=S_{N}=m,S_{n-1}=i,S_{n}=j\right]}{\sum_{m=1}^{M}P\left[S_{0}=S_{N}=m,S_{n-1}=i\right]}\\
&=\frac{\sum_{m=1}^{M}\mu_{m}\left[\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}P_{k}\right]_{m,i}\left[P_{n}\right]_{i,j}\left[\prod_{k=n+1}^{N}P_{k}\right]_{j,m}}{\sum_{m=1}^{M}\mu_{m}\left[\prod_{k=1}^{n-1}P_{k}\right]_{m,i}\left[\prod_{k=n}^{N}P_{k}\right]_{i,m}}.\end{aligned}`$ |  |

Suppose $`\mu`$ is uniform and that
$`\big[P_{n}\big]_{i,j}=\alpha\left(\delta_{n}\right)\mathbb{I}\{i=j\}+\beta\left(\delta_{n}\right)\mathbb{I}\{i\neq`$
$`j\}`$ with $`\delta_{n}\in[0,1]`$ for each $`n\in[N]`$, where

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\alpha(\delta)=\frac{1+(M-1)\delta}{M},\beta(\delta)=\frac{1-\delta}{M}.
``` |  |

Then
$`\big[\tilde{P}_{n}\big]_{i,j}=\alpha(\tilde{\delta}_{n})\mathbb{I}\{i=j\}+\beta(\tilde{\delta}_{n})\mathbb{I}\{i\neq j\}`$
satisfies

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tilde{\epsilon}_{n}=\frac{1-\prod_{k\neq n}\delta_{k}}{1+(M-1)\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{k}}\epsilon_{n},
``` |  | (4) |

where $`\tilde{\epsilon}_{n}=1-\tilde{\delta}_{n}`$ and
$`\epsilon_{n}=1-\delta_{n}`$.

###### Proof.

Let $`\left\{u_{m}\right\}_{m=1}^{M}`$ be an orthonormal basis of
$`\mathbb{R}^{M}`$ where $`u_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\mathbf{1}`$. Then

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle P_{n}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\delta_{n}I_{M}+\tfrac{1-\delta_{n}}{M}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\delta_{n}\sum_{m=1}^{M}u_{m}u_{m}^{\top}+\left(1-\delta_{n}\right)u_{1}u_{1}^{\top}`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=u_{1}u_{1}^{\top}+\delta_{n}\sum_{m=2}^{M}u_{m}u_{m}^{\top}=U\Lambda_{n}U^{\top},`$ |  |

where $`U=\left[u_{1}\cdots u_{M}\right]`$ and
$`\Lambda_{n}=\operatorname{diag}\left(1,\delta_{n},\cdots,\delta_{n}\right)`$.
Denote $`\delta_{k:l}=\prod_{t=k}^{l}\delta_{t}`$ and $`\Lambda_{k:l}=`$
$`\prod_{t=k}^{l}\Lambda_{t}=\delta_{k:l}I_{M}+\left(1-\delta_{k:l}\right)e_{1}e_{1}^{\top}`$.
One has

[TABLE]

Note that

[TABLE]

are identical for all $`i\neq j`$. Hence there uniquely exists a
$`\tilde{\delta}_{n}\in[0,1]`$ such that
$`\big[\tilde{P}_{n}\big]_{i,j}=\beta\big(\tilde{\delta}_{n}\big)`$ and
$`\big[\tilde{P}_{n}\big]_{i,i}=\alpha\big(\tilde{\delta}_{n}\big)`$ for
all $`i\neq j`$. Moreover, (cf.
([5](#A1.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ Proof. ‣ A.2.6 Propositions for Proving the Main Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")))

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |   $`\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \alpha\big(\tilde{\delta}_{n}\big)&=\alpha\left(\delta_{n}\right)\frac{(M-1)\beta\left(\delta_{1:n-1}\right)\beta\left(\delta_{n+1:N}\right)+\alpha\left(\delta_{1:n-1}\right)\alpha\left(\delta_{n+1,N}\right)}{(M-1)\beta\left(\delta_{1:n-1}\right)\beta\left(\delta_{n:N}\right)+\alpha\left(\delta_{1:n-1}\right)\alpha\left(\delta_{n,N}\right)}\\
&=\alpha\left(\delta_{n}\right)\frac{\left(1-\alpha\left(\delta_{1:n-1}\right)\right)\beta\left(\delta_{n+1:N}\right)+\alpha\left(\delta_{1:n-1}\right)\alpha\left(\delta_{n+1,N}\right)}{\left(1-\alpha\left(\delta_{1:n-1}\right)\right)\beta\left(\delta_{n:N}\right)+\alpha\left(\delta_{1:n-1}\right)\alpha\left(\delta_{n,N}\right)}\\
&=\alpha\left(\delta_{n}\right)\frac{\beta\left(\delta_{n+1:N}\right)+\alpha\left(\delta_{1:n-1}\right)\delta_{n+1:N}}{\beta\left(\delta_{n:N}\right)+\alpha\left(\delta_{1:n-1}\right)\delta_{n:N}}\\
&=\alpha\left(\delta_{n}\right)\frac{1+(M-1)\delta_{1:n-1}\delta_{n+1:N}}{1+(M-1)\delta_{1:N}}.\end{aligned}`$ |  |

Hence,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |   $`\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &(M-1)\beta\big(\tilde{\delta}_{n}\big)=1-\left(1-(M-1)\beta\left(\delta_{n}\right)\right)\frac{1+(M-1)\delta_{1:n-1}\delta_{n+1:N}}{1+(M-1)\delta_{1:N}}\\
&=\frac{(M-1)\left(\delta_{1:N}-\delta_{1:n-1}\delta_{n+1:N}\right)+(M-1)\beta\left(\delta_{n}\right)\left(1+(M-1)\delta_{1:n-1}\delta_{n+1:N}\right)}{1+(M-1)\delta_{1:N}}\\
&=\frac{(M-1)\left(-M\beta\left(\delta_{n}\right)\delta_{1:n-1}\delta_{n+1:N}\right)+(M-1)\beta\left(\delta_{n}\right)\left(1+(M-1)\delta_{1:n-1}\delta_{n+1:N}\right)}{1+(M-1)\delta_{1:N}}\\
&=(M-1)\beta\left(\delta_{n}\right)\frac{1-\delta_{1:n-1}\delta_{n+1:N}}{1+(M-1)\delta_{1:N}}.\end{aligned}`$ |  |

Note that $`\epsilon_{n}=M\beta\left(\delta_{n}\right)`$ and
$`\tilde{\epsilon}_{n}=M\beta\big(\tilde{\delta}_{n}\big)`$ yield
Eq. ([4](#A1.E4 "Equation 4 ‣ Proposition A.1. ‣ A.2.6 Propositions for Proving the Main Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")).
∎

###### Proposition A.2.

Consider the scenario defined in
Proposition [A.1](#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Proposition A.1. ‣ A.2.6 Propositions for Proving the Main Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
Let
$`\left(\theta_{t}\right)_{t=0}^{\infty},\left(\vartheta_{t}\right)_{t=0}^{\infty}`$
be two non-negative non-increasing sequences satisfying
$`\vartheta_{t}\leq\theta_{t}`$, $`\vartheta_{0}\in(0,1)`$, and

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta_{t+1}\leq\frac{\vartheta_{t}}{M-(M-1)\vartheta_{t}}\theta_{t}.
``` |  |

We have the following:

1.  (a)
    Denote $`\theta=\sum_{k=1}^{N}(1-\delta_{k})`$ and
    $`\vartheta=1-\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{k}`$. Then,
    $`\vartheta\leq\theta`$.
2.  (b)
    Following $`(a)`$, if we further assume $`\delta_{n}>0`$ for all
    $`n`$, we have

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \sum_{k=1}^{N}\tilde{\epsilon}_{k}\leq\frac{\vartheta\theta}{M-(M-1)\vartheta}.
    ``` |  |
3.  (c)
    Denote
    $`\gamma=\frac{\vartheta_{0}}{M-(M-1)\vartheta_{0}}\in(0,1)`$. Then
    $`\theta_{t}\leq\gamma^{t}\theta_{0}`$. That is, for
    $`\varepsilon>0`$, it holds that $`\theta_{t}\leq\varepsilon`$
    whenever
    $`t\geq\frac{\log\left(\theta_{0}/\varepsilon\right)}{\log(1/\gamma)}\vee 0`$.
4.  (d)
    If $`\theta_{0}<\frac{M}{M+1}`$, then

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \theta_{t}\leq\frac{M\left(\theta_{0}\right)^{2^{t}}}{M\left(\theta_{0}\right)^{2^{t}}+\left(M\left(1-\theta_{0}\right)\right)^{2^{t}}}.
    ``` |  |

    Furthermore, for $`\varepsilon\in\left(0,\frac{M}{M+1}\right)`$, it
    holds that $`\theta_{t}\leq\varepsilon`$ whenever

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    t\geq\operatorname{max}\left(\log_{2}\left(\frac{\log M+\log\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}}{\log M+\log\frac{1-\theta_{0}}{\theta_{0}}}\right),\,0\right).
    ``` |  |
5.  (e)
    For $`\varepsilon\in\left(0,\frac{M}{M+1}\right)`$, we have
    $`\theta_{t}\leq\varepsilon`$ whenever

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |   $`\displaystyle t\geq\left\lceil\frac{\log\frac{M+1}{M\gamma}+\log\left(\theta_{0}\right)}{\log(1/\gamma)}\right\rceil_{+}+\left\lceil\log_{2}\left(\frac{\log M+\log\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}}{\log\frac{(M+1)-M\gamma}{\gamma}}\right)\right\rceil_{+}.`$ |  |

###### Proof.

1.  (a)
    Because $`0\leq\delta_{k}\leq 1`$ for all $`k\in[N]`$, we can use a
    probability space $`(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mu)`$ to show
    $`\vartheta\leq\theta`$. Let
    $`\{E_{1},E_{2},\dots,E_{N}\}\subset\mathcal{F}`$ be events with
    $`\mu(E_{k})=\delta_{k}`$. Then the complements $`E_{k}^{c}`$
    satisfy $`\mu(E_{k}^{c})=1-\delta_{k}`$. We can define

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \vartheta=\mu\!\Bigl(\bigcup_{k=1}^{N}E_{k}^{c}\Bigr)\quad\text{and}\quad\theta=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mu(E_{k}^{c}).
    ``` |  |

    If $`E_{1}^{c},E_{2}^{c},\dots,E_{N}^{c}`$ are disjoint,
    $`\vartheta=\theta`$ by countable additivity. In general,
    $`E_{k}^{c}`$ may overlap, so

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \mu\Bigl(\bigcup_{k=1}^{N}E_{k}^{c}\Bigr)\leq\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mu(E_{k}^{c}),
    ``` |  |

    implying $`\vartheta\leq\theta`$.
2.  (b)
    From the proof of
    Proposition [A.1](#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Proposition A.1. ‣ A.2.6 Propositions for Proving the Main Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
    we can derive

    [TABLE]

    where the inequalities follow by noting that $`\vartheta\leq\theta`$
    and

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |   $`\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\theta^{2}=\left(\sum_{k=1}^{N}\frac{\epsilon_{k}}{\sqrt{1-\epsilon_{k}}}\cdot\sqrt{1-\epsilon_{k}}\right)^{2}\leq\left(\sum_{k=1}^{N}\frac{\epsilon_{k}^{2}}{1-\epsilon_{k}}\right)\left(\sum_{k=1}^{N}\left(1-\epsilon_{k}\right)\right)=(N-\theta)\sum_{k=1}^{N}\frac{\epsilon_{k}^{2}}{1-\epsilon_{k}}\\
    \Rightarrow&\sum_{k=1}^{N}\frac{\epsilon_{k}}{1-\epsilon_{k}}=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\left(\epsilon_{k}+\frac{\epsilon_{k}^{2}}{1-\epsilon_{k}}\right)\geq\theta+\frac{\theta^{2}}{N-\theta}=\frac{N\theta}{N-\theta}.\end{aligned}`$ |  |
3.  (c)
    Since $`\vartheta_{t}\leq\vartheta_{0}`$, it is clear that
    $`\theta_{t+1}\leq\gamma\theta_{t}`$ and the rest is trivial.
4.  (d)
    Denote $`f:x\in[0,1]\mapsto\frac{x^{2}}{M-(M-1)x}`$ and
    $`g:x\in[0,1)\mapsto\left(\varphi\circ h\circ\varphi^{-1}\right)(x)`$
    where

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |   $`\displaystyle\varphi:x\in[0,\infty)\mapsto\frac{Mx}{Mx+1},\quad h:x\in[0,\infty)\mapsto x^{2},\quad\varphi^{-1}:y\in[0,1)\mapsto\frac{y}{M(1-y)}.`$ |  |

    Note that

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |   $`\displaystyle g(x)=\frac{M\left(\frac{x}{M(1-x)}\right)^{2}}{M\left(\frac{x}{M(1-x)}\right)^{2}+1}=\frac{x^{2}}{M-2Mx+(M+1)x^{2}}\geq\frac{x^{2}}{M-2Mx+(M+1)x}=f(x),`$ |  |

    for all $`x\in[0,1)`$. Since $`\vartheta_{t}\leq\theta_{t}<1`$, one
    has
    $`\theta_{t+1}\leq f\left(\theta_{t}\right)\leq g\left(\theta_{t}\right)`$,
    which further implies
    $`\theta_{t}\leq g^{(t)}\left(\theta_{0}\right)`$ due to $`g`$ being
    monotonically increasing. Thus

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \theta_{t}\leq g^{(t)}\left(\theta_{0}\right)=\left(\varphi\circ h^{(t)}\circ\varphi^{-1}\right)\left(\theta_{0}\right)=\frac{M\left(\frac{\theta_{0}}{M\left(1-\theta_{0}\right)}\right)^{2^{t}}}{M\left(\frac{\theta_{0}}{M\left(1-\theta_{0}\right)}\right)^{2^{t}}+1}.
    ``` |  |

    We complete the proof by noting that (provided $`t\geq 0`$)

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |   $`\displaystyle\begin{aligned} g^{(t)}\left(\theta_{0}\right)\leq\varepsilon&\Leftrightarrow\left(\varphi\circ h^{(t)}\circ\varphi^{-1}\right)\left(\theta_{0}\right)\leq\varepsilon\Leftrightarrow\left(\varphi^{-1}\left(\theta_{0}\right)\right)^{2^{t}}=\left(h^{(t)}\circ\varphi^{-1}\right)\left(\theta_{0}\right)\leq\varphi^{-1}(\varepsilon)\\
    &\Leftrightarrow 2^{t}\log\left(1/\varphi^{-1}\left(\theta_{0}\right)\right)\geq\log\left(1/\varphi^{-1}(\varepsilon)\right)\Leftrightarrow t\geq\log_{2}\left(\frac{\log\left(1/\varphi^{-1}(\varepsilon)\right)}{\log\left(1/\varphi^{-1}\left(\theta_{0}\right)\right)}\right).\end{aligned}`$ |  |
5.  (e)
    Take

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |   $`\displaystyle\tau_{1}=\left\lceil\frac{\log\frac{M+1}{M\gamma}+\log\left(\theta_{0}\right)}{\log(1/\gamma)}\right\rceil_{+}\!\!,~\tau_{2}=\left\lceil\log_{2}\left(\frac{\log M+\log\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}}{\log\frac{M+1-M\gamma}{\gamma}}\right)\right\rceil_{+}\!\!.`$ |  |

    Then (a) implies $`\theta_{\tau_{1}}\leq\frac{M\gamma}{M+1}`$,
    and (b) further implies
    $`\theta_{\tau_{1}+\tau_{2}}\leq\varepsilon`$.

∎

#### A.2.7 Proof of Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")

###### Proof.

The proof of this theorem is based primarily on
Proposition [A.1](#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Proposition A.1. ‣ A.2.6 Propositions for Proving the Main Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
Without loss of generality, we assume that
$`s_{0,m}=s_{1,m}=\cdots=s_{N,m}=m`$ for every $`m\in[M]`$ and only
consider the first iteration of RL-STaR (i.e., $`t=1`$ and $`t-1=0`$).
We omit subscripts $`(0,n)`$ and simply write $`P_{0,n}=P_{n}`$,
$`\delta_{0,n}=\delta_{n}`$, and $`S_{0,n}=S_{n}`$, etc. Similarly, let
$`P_{1,n}=\tilde{P}_{n}`$, $`\delta_{1,n}=\tilde{\delta}_{n}`$,
$`\tilde{\epsilon}_{n}=1-\delta_{1,n}`$, and
$`\epsilon_{n}=1-\delta_{n}`$, etc. Under this formulation, the scenario
given in
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
can be seen as the Markov process introduced in
Proposition [A.1](#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Proposition A.1. ‣ A.2.6 Propositions for Proving the Main Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
Applying
Eq. ([4](#A1.E4 "Equation 4 ‣ Proposition A.1. ‣ A.2.6 Propositions for Proving the Main Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")),
we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\delta_{t,n}=\frac{(M-2)\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{t-1,k}+\prod_{k\neq n}\delta_{t-1,k}+\delta_{t-1,n}}{1+(M-1)\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{t-1,k}}.
``` |  | (6) |

We now examine the three cases with respect to the values of
$`\delta_{t=1,n}`$.

1.  (a)
    If $`0<\delta_{0,n}<1`$ for all $`n\in[N]`$, it is obvious that
    $`0<\tilde{\epsilon}_{n}<\epsilon_{n}`$ and hence

    |     |                              |     |
    |-----|------------------------------|-----|
    |     |
           ``` math
           \delta_{0,n}<\delta_{1,n}<1.
           ```                           |     |

    It is straightforward that this inequality will hold for every
    subsequent iteration $`t>1`$.
2.  (b)
    Suppose there exists an $`n\in[N]`$ such that $`\delta_{0,n}=0`$ and
    for any other $`n^{\prime}\neq n,~n^{\prime}\in[N]`$ we have
    $`\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}>0`$. Then,
    $`\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{0,k}=0`$,
    $`\prod_{n^{\prime}\neq n}\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}>0`$ and
    $`\prod_{k\neq n^{\prime}}\delta_{0,k}=0`$ for any
    $`k\neq n^{\prime},n^{\prime}\neq n,~k,n^{\prime}\in[N]`$. One now
    sees that

    |  |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|----|
    |  | $`\displaystyle\delta_{1,n}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{0+\prod_{n^{\prime}\neq n}\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}+0}{1+0}=\prod_{n^{\prime}\neq n}\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}>0,`$ |  |
    |  | $`\displaystyle\delta_{1,n^{\prime}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{0+0+\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}}{1+0}=\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}>0.`$ |  |

    After the first iteration, apply the analysis in $`(a)`$.
3.  (c)
    Suppose there exist two (or more than two) steps
    $`n,n^{\prime}\in[N]`$ satisfying $`n^{\prime}\neq n`$,
    $`\delta_{0,n}=0`$ and $`\delta_{0,n^{\prime}}=0`$. We have
    $`\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{0,k}=0`$, and
    $`\prod_{k\neq n}\delta_{0,k}=0`$ for any $`k\in[N]`$. Then

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \delta_{1,n}=\frac{0+0+\delta_{0,n}}{1+0}=\delta_{0,n}\quad\text{for all $n\in[N]$}.
    ``` |  |

    It is obvious that above equation holds for every subsequent
    iteration $`t>1`$.

∎

#### A.2.8 Proof of Theorem [4.10](#S4.Thmtheorem10 "Theorem 4.10 (Convergence Speed of 𝛿_{𝑡,𝑛}). ‣ Proof. ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")

###### Proof.

For the case of $`\delta_{0,n}>0`$ for all $`n\in[N]`$, we can apply
Proposition [A.2](#A1.Thmtheorem2 "Proposition A.2. ‣ Proof. ‣ A.2.6 Propositions for Proving the Main Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
where we set

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\gamma=\frac{\vartheta_{0}}{M-(M-1)\vartheta_{0}}=\frac{1-\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{0,k}}{(M-1)\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{0,k}+1},
``` |  |

and let $`\varepsilon=\frac{\varepsilon^{\prime}}{N}`$ for
$`\varepsilon^{\prime}\in\left(0,\frac{M}{M+1}\right)`$. Therefore,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\max_{k}\delta_{t,k}\geq\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{t,k}}{N}\geq 1-\frac{\varepsilon^{\prime}}{N}
``` |  |

holds for all

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |   $`\displaystyle t\geq\left\lceil\frac{\log\frac{M+1}{M\gamma}+\log\left(\theta_{0}\right)}{\log(1/\gamma)}\right\rceil_{+}+\left\lceil\log_{2}\left(\frac{\log M+\log\frac{1-\varepsilon^{\prime}}{\varepsilon^{\prime}}}{\log\frac{(M+1)-M\gamma}{\gamma}}\right)\right\rceil_{+}.`$ |  |

On the other hand, if there exists only one $`n\in[N]`$ such that
$`\delta_{0,n}=0`$, an additional iteration $`t=1`$ is needed to ensure
$`\delta_{1,n}>0`$. Once $`\delta_{1,n}`$ becomes strictly positive for
all $`n\in[N]`$, we set

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\gamma=\frac{1-\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{1,k}}{(M-1)\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{1,k}+1},
``` |  |

and then the argument proceeds as before, completing the proof. ∎

#### A.2.9 Proof of Corollary [4.11](#S4.Thmtheorem11 "Corollary 4.11 (Policy Improvement). ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof. ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")

###### Proof.

By applying
Proposition [A.1](#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Proposition A.1. ‣ A.2.6 Propositions for Proving the Main Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
to the $`t`$-th iteration of RL-STaR, we abuse the notation of
$`P_{t,n}`$ to denote the transition matrix in the $`t`$-th iteration of
RL-STaR, at the $`n`$-th CoT step. Recall that

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |   $`\displaystyle\prod_{k=1}^{N}P_{t,k}=U\left(\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{t,k}I_{M}+\big(1-\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{t,k}\big)e_{1}e_{1}^{\top}\right)U^{T},`$ |  |

where $`U=[u_{1},u_{2},\dots,u_{M}]`$, and
$`u_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\mathbf{1}`$. One sees that

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |   $`\displaystyle\big[\prod_{k=1}^{N}P_{t,k}\big]_{i,i}=\big[\prod_{k=1}^{N}P_{(t,k)}\big]_{1,1}=\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{t,k}+\frac{1-\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{t,k}}{M}.`$ |  |

Since the initial state is chosen uniformly,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |   $`\displaystyle J(P_{t})=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{1}{M}\big[\prod_{k=1}^{N}P_{(t,k)}\big]_{m,m}=\frac{1}{M}+\tfrac{M-1}{M}\prod_{k=1}^{N}\delta_{t,k}.`$ |  |

Assuming
Theorem [4.9](#S4.Thmtheorem9 "Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner") [(a)](#S4.I3.i1 "Item (a) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
or
[(b)](#S4.I3.i2 "Item (b) ‣ Theorem 4.9 (Sufficient Conditions of Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
hold, we conclude as $`\delta_{1,n}\geq\delta_{0,n}`$ and
$`\delta_{t,n}>\delta_{t-1,n}`$ for all $`t>1`$ and $`n\in[N]`$.∎

#### A.2.10 Proof of Corollary [4.12](#S4.Thmtheorem12 "Corollary 4.12 (Convergence to the Optimal Policy). ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof. ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")

###### Proof.

Theorem [4.10](#S4.Thmtheorem10 "Theorem 4.10 (Convergence Speed of 𝛿_{𝑡,𝑛}). ‣ Proof. ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
implies that

|     |                                                               |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \lim_{t\to\infty}\delta_{t,n}=1\quad\text{for all $n\in[N]$}.
       ```                                                            |     |

By
Proposition [A.1](#A1.Thmtheorem1 "Proposition A.1. ‣ A.2.6 Propositions for Proving the Main Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
we know that $`P_{t,n}`$ has diagonal elements $`\alpha(\delta_{t,n})`$
and off-diagonal elements $`\beta(\delta_{t,n})`$ such that

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}\alpha(\delta_{t,n})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{1+(M-1)\delta_{t,n}}{M}=1,`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}\beta(\delta_{t,n})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{1-\delta_{t,n}}{M}=0,`$ |  |

for all $`n\in[N]`$. Every row of $`P_{t,n}-I_{M}`$ has one entry equal
to $`\alpha(\delta_{t,n})-1`$ and $`M-1`$ entries equal to
$`\beta(\delta_{t,n})`$, so
$`\|P_{t,n}-I_{M}\|_{\infty}=\left(1-\alpha(\delta_{t,n})\right)+(M-1)\beta(\delta_{t,n})`$.
Hence,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}\|P_{t,n}-I_{M}\|_{\infty}=0\quad\text{for all}\quad n\in[N].
``` |  |

∎

#### A.2.11 Proof of Corollary [4.13](#S4.Thmtheorem13 "Corollary 4.13 (Diminishing of Incorrect Reasoning Trajectories). ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof. ‣ Proof. ‣ 4.4 Main Theorem ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")

###### Proof.

This is a simple consequence of convergence to the optimal policy. Since
the incorrect reasoning steps may appear in any CoT steps, we see that

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p(\tau_{t,k})=\frac{1}{M}\left(\beta(\delta_{t,n_{1}})\cdots(\beta(\delta_{t,n_{k}})\right)\prod_{j\neq n_{i}\forall i}\alpha(\delta_{t,j})
``` |  |

where $`2\leq k\leq N`$, for some subsequence
$`n_{1}<n_{2}<\cdots<n_{k}`$. Using
$`\lim_{t\to\infty}\alpha(\delta_{t,n})=1`$ and
$`\lim_{t\to\infty}\beta(\delta_{t,n})=0`$ for each $`n`$, we have
$`0\leq p(\tau_{t,k})\xrightarrow{t\to\infty}0`$. Because
$`|\bigcup_{k}\tau_{t,k}|<\infty`$, we obtain the desired result. ∎

### A.3 Toy Example without the Markov Assumption

In the toy example of
Sec. [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
let $`P_{0,n}`$ denote the pre-trained LLM’s estimated transition at
step $`n`$, which fails to satisfy the Markov property. Specifically, we
assume

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle P_{0,1}(S_{1}|S_{0})=\begin{cases}\frac{1+\delta_{0,n}}{2}&\text{if }(S_{1},S_{0})=(s_{1,m},s_{0,m})\text{ for all }n,m\in[2],\\
\frac{1-\delta_{0,n}}{2}&\text{otherwise. }\end{cases}`$ |  |

And that

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle P_{0,2}(S_{2}|S_{1},S_{0})=\begin{cases}\frac{(1+\delta_{0,1})^{2}}{4}&\text{if }(S_{2},S_{1},S_{0})=(s_{2,m},s_{1,m},s_{0,m})\text{ for all }m\in[2],\\
\frac{(1+\delta_{0,1})(1-\delta_{0,2})}{4}&\text{if }(S_{2},S_{1},S_{0})=(s_{2,m^{\prime}\neq m},s_{1,m},s_{0,m})\text{ for all }m^{\prime},m\in[2],\\
\frac{(1-\delta_{0,1})(1+\delta_{0,2})}{4}&\text{if }(S_{2},S_{1},S_{0})=(s_{2,m},s_{1,m},s_{0,m^{\prime}\neq m})\text{ for all }m^{\prime},m\in[2],\\
\frac{(1-\delta_{0,1})^{2}}{2}&\text{if }(S_{2},S_{1},S_{0})=(s_{2,m},s_{1,m^{\prime}\neq m},s_{0,m})\text{ for all }m^{\prime},m\in[2].\end{cases}`$ |  |

To derive $`P_{1}(S_{1}\mid S_{0})`$ and
$`P_{2}(S_{2}\mid S_{1},S_{0})`$, we follow the same procedure as in the
proof of
Theorem [4.4](#S4.Thmtheorem4 "Theorem 4.4 (Sufficient Conditions for Pre-trained Models). ‣ 4.3 A Toy Example ‣ 4 Theoretical Results ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
in [A.2.1](#A1.SS2.SSS1 "A.2.1 Proof of Theorem ‣ A.2 Proof of Theorems ‣ Appendix A Appendix ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner").
In the inner loop $`\ell=1,\dots,L`$ of
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 3 Theoretical Framework ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner"),
we sample trajectories $`\tau`$, and each occurring with probability
$`p(\tau)`$ as

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p(\tau)=\begin{cases}.125\left({1+\delta_{0,1}}\right)\left({1+\delta_{0,2}}\right)&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,1},s_{1,1},s_{2,1}),\\
.125\left({1+\delta_{0,1}}\right)\left({1-\delta_{0,2}}\right)&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,1},s_{1,1},s_{2,2}),\\
.125\left({1-\delta_{0,1}}\right)\left({1-\delta_{0,2}}\right)&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,1},s_{1,2},s_{2,1}),\\
.125\left({1-\delta_{0,1}}\right)\left({1+\delta_{0,2}}\right)&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,1},s_{1,2},s_{2,2}),\\
.125\left({1-\delta_{0,1}}\right)\left({1+\delta_{0,2}}\right)&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,2},s_{1,1},s_{2,1}),\\
.125\left({1-\delta_{0,1}}\right)\left({1-\delta_{0,2}}\right)&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,2},s_{1,1},s_{2,2}),\\
.125\left({1+\delta_{0,1}}\right)\left({1-\delta_{0,2}}\right)&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,2},s_{1,2},s_{2,1}),\\
.125\left({1+\delta_{0,1}}\right)\left({1+\delta_{0,2}}\right)&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,2},s_{1,2},s_{2,2}).\\
\end{cases}
``` |  |

Conditioned on $`\tau\in\mathcal{D}_{1}`$, the sampling probability is
$`p(\tau\mid\tau\in\mathcal{D}_{1})`$ as

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p(\tau|\tau\in\mathcal{D}_{1})=\begin{cases}\frac{(1+\delta_{0,1})(1+\delta_{0,2})}{4(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,1},s_{1,1},s_{2,1}),\\
\frac{(1-\delta_{0,1})(1-\delta_{0,2})}{4(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,1},s_{1,2},s_{2,1}),\\
\frac{(1-\delta_{0,1})(1-\delta_{0,2})}{4(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,2},s_{1,1},s_{2,2}),\\
\frac{(1+\delta_{0,1})(1+\delta_{0,2})}{4(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}&\text{if }\tau=(s_{0,2},s_{1,2},s_{2,2}).\\
\end{cases}
``` |  |

If the LLM perfectly learns these conditional transitions from
$`\tau\sim p(\tau\mid\tau\in\mathcal{D}_{1})`$, then

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle P_{1,1}(S_{1}|S_{0})=\begin{cases}\frac{(1+\delta_{0,1})(1+\delta_{0,2})}{2(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}&\text{if $(S_{1},S_{0})=(s_{1,m},s_{0,m})$ for all $m\in[2]$},\\
\frac{(1-\delta_{0,1})(1-\delta_{0,2})}{2(1+\delta_{0,1}\delta_{0,2})}&\text{if $(S_{1},S_{0})=(s_{1,m^{\prime}\neq m},s_{0,m})$ for all $m^{\prime},m\in[2]$}.\end{cases}`$ |  |

And that

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle P_{1,2}(S_{2}|S_{1},S_{0})=\begin{cases}1&\text{if $(S_{2},S_{1},S_{0})\in$}\text{$\left\{(s_{2,m},s_{1,m},s_{0,m}),(s_{2,m},s_{1,m^{\prime}\neq m},s_{0,m})\right\}$}\text{ for all $m^{\prime},m\in[2]$},\\
0&\text{if $(S_{2},S_{1},S_{0})\in$}\text{$\left\{(s_{2,m\neq m^{\prime}},s_{1,m},s_{0,m}),(s_{2,m},s_{1,m},s_{0,m^{\prime}\neq m})\right\}$}\text{ for all $m^{\prime},m\in[2]$}.\\
\end{cases}`$ |  |

Based on these equations, since $`P_{1,2}`$ is deterministic, repeating
the outer loop of
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.1 Problem Formulation ‣ 3 Theoretical Framework ‣ RL-STaR: Theoretical Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Frameworks for Self-Taught Reasoner")
for $`T`$ iterations yields
$`\mathcal{D}_{T}=\mathcal{D}_{T-1}=\cdots=\mathcal{D}_{1}`$. As a
result, the trajectories
$`\tau=(s_{0,m},s_{1,m^{\prime}\neq m},s_{2,m})`$, which contain an
incorrect reasoning step, remain in the dataset and cannot be removed by
RL-STaR.
````
